modules.title: Managing complexity
modules.summary: Learn to see complexity as a cost other people pay, and design modules, names and comments that keep that cost low.

lessons.title: What complexity actually is
lessons.objective: By the end you can name the three symptoms of complexity (change amplification, cognitive load, unknown unknowns) and point to a real instance of each in code you wrote.
concept: John Ousterhout defines complexity as anything about the structure of a system that makes it hard to understand and modify. It is not line count or clever algorithms: a 300-line module can be simple and a 20-line one can be a trap. Complexity is measured by the people who work with the code. If a change that should take ten minutes takes a day because you had to read six files first and still broke something, the system is complex, however elegant it looked to its author.

It shows up as three symptoms. **Change amplification**: a simple change needs edits in many places, like a free-shipping threshold written as `>= 50` in four files. **Cognitive load**: how much you must hold in your head to change something safely, such as remembering that `save()` must always follow `validate()`. **Unknown unknowns**: it is not obvious which code must change or what you need to know, so the change passes review and breaks production. The third is the worst, because you cannot even estimate it.

Ousterhout names two root causes: **dependencies** (code that cannot be understood or changed in isolation) and **obscurity** (important information that is not obvious). Complexity is incremental. No single commit ruins a codebase, but every "just this once" shortcut adds a little, and the total compounds. That is why he argues for **strategic programming**, investing roughly 10 to 20 percent of your time in design improvements, over **tactical programming**, where the only goal is to get the current feature working as fast as possible.

lessons.tryit: Pick a project you shipped in the previous stage. Find one concrete instance of each symptom: a change that would need edits in several files, a function whose caller must remember an unwritten rule, and a place where a newcomer would not know what else to change. Write each as `symptom / file:line / why it hurts / one-sentence fix`.

questions.prompt: Which situation is an example of an **unknown unknown**?
options: Changing the session timeout also requires updating a hard-coded value in a cron job that nobody mentions anywhere, so the first deploy logs everyone out
Renaming a column requires editing 14 SQL queries, and the compiler points to all of them
A function takes nine positional arguments, so every call needs the docs open
A 2,000-line file takes a long time to scroll through
questions.explain: Unknown unknowns are cases where you cannot tell what else must change or what you need to know. The cron job's dependency is invisible until it breaks. The 14 queries are change amplification, but a known one: the tooling shows you every site. Nine positional arguments raise cognitive load. File length alone is not one of the three symptoms.

questions.prompt: The free-shipping threshold was raised from 50 to 60 last week. What does this print?
questions.explain: `banner` still has the old literal `50`, so a $55 cart is told shipping is free, while `shipping_cost` uses the new constant and charges 5.99. This is change amplification turning into a bug: the rule existed in two places and only one was updated. The fix is to make `banner` use `FREE_SHIPPING` too, or better, a single `qualifies_for_free_shipping(total)` function.

questions.prompt: Which design is better for the 30 places in your app that write to the database, and why?
questions.code:
# Design A
conn.begin()
try:
    conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?", (amt, src))
    conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?", (amt, dst))
    conn.commit()
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    raise

# Design B
with db.transaction() as tx:   # commits on success, rolls back and re-raises on error
    tx.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?", (amt, src))
    tx.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?", (amt, dst))
options: A, because B hides errors inside the context manager
They are equivalent; B is only shorter
A, because explicit calls make every step visible to the reader
B, because the module, not every caller, now holds the rule that a failure must roll back, which removes a piece of cognitive load and a way to leave a transaction open
questions.explain: In A, each of the 30 call sites must remember begin, commit, and rollback on every error path; forgetting the rollback once leaves a dangling transaction. B moves that knowledge into one place, and the `with` block still lets exceptions propagate after rolling back, so it hides nothing the caller needs. Shorter is a side effect: the real gain is that a rule callers had to remember is now enforced for them.

questions.prompt: A teammate says: "I'll copy the validation logic into the new endpoint for now and clean it up later." In Ousterhout's terms this is:
options: Strategic programming, because it ships the feature
Neither, because duplication is not complexity
Information hiding, because each endpoint owns its own copy
Tactical programming: it is fast today and adds a little complexity (duplicated rules) that every future change to validation will pay for
questions.explain: Tactical programming optimizes for finishing the current task. The copy creates change amplification: the next rule change must be made twice, and the person making it may not know about the second copy. Duplication is a classic source of complexity, and two copies of one rule are the opposite of information hiding, where one module owns a decision.

lessons.title: Deep vs shallow modules
lessons.objective: By the end you can judge whether a module is deep or shallow by comparing its interface to the work it hides, and redesign a call site so the common case is one line.
concept: Picture each module (function, class, package, service) as a rectangle. The top edge is its **interface**: everything a caller must know to use it, including parameters, return values, side effects and ordering rules. The area is its **functionality**: the work it does for you. A **deep** module hides a lot of functionality behind a small interface. Unix file I/O is the classic case: five calls (`open`, `read`, `write`, `lseek`, `close`) hide disk layout, caching, permissions and device drivers. The interface is the cost; the functionality is the benefit.

A **shallow** module has an interface almost as complicated as what it does. A wrapper that renames `requests.get` to `http_get` and adds nothing, or a class whose only method sets one field, makes callers learn a new name without taking any work off them. Ousterhout calls the habit of splitting everything into tiny classes **classitis**. Each piece looks simple, but the system now has more interfaces to learn, more files to open, and more places for knowledge to leak between pieces.

Depth is about the **common case**. Python's `open(path)` defaults to text mode with sensible buffering; you meet `buffering=` or `newline=` only when you need them. Older Java required wrapping a `FileInputStream` in a `BufferedInputStream` in an `InputStreamReader`, so every caller paid for flexibility most never used. A practical test: write the call site first. If the common use needs more than a line or two, or needs the caller to supply knowledge the module already has, the module is too shallow.

left.title: Deep module
points: Small interface, lots of hidden work
Common case is one call with defaults
Callers do not need to know internals
Example: open(), json.loads(), SQLite

right.title: Shallow module
points: Interface nearly as big as the body
Every caller repeats the same setup steps
Pass-through wrappers that rename things
Example: get_name(user), classitis

example.code:
# Shallow: every caller orchestrates the same five steps
reader = ConfigFileReader("app.toml")
raw = reader.read_text()
data = TomlParser().parse(raw)
merged = EnvOverlay(prefix="APP_").apply(data)
port = int(merged["server"]["port"])

# Deep: one call, same functionality hidden inside
config = load_config("app.toml")   # reads, parses, overlays APP_* env vars, validates types
port = config.server.port          # already an int
example.explain: Both versions do the same work. In the shallow version the file format, the env-variable prefix and the type conversion leak into every caller. In the deep version they are `load_config`'s secret, so changing the prefix or moving to YAML touches one function.

lessons.tryit: Find the most-used class or module in one of your own projects and draw it as a rectangle: list its public methods and parameters along the top and the responsibilities it hides inside. Then write the call site you wish you had for the most common use, and mark which parameters or steps could become defaults or move inside.

questions.prompt: In Ousterhout's terms, a **deep** module is one that:
options: Provides a lot of functionality through a small, simple interface
Has many layers of inheritance
Exposes every internal option so callers have full control
Is split into many small classes, each with one method
questions.explain: Depth is the ratio of functionality to interface. Inheritance depth is unrelated. Many one-method classes is classitis, which tends to produce shallow modules. Exposing every option makes the interface large, which is the cost side of the ratio.

questions.prompt: `pathlib` is a deep module: one object hides string splitting, separators and edge cases. What does this print?
questions.code:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath

p = PurePosixPath("/srv/app/logs/today.log")
print(p.suffix, p.parent.name)
questions.explain: `suffix` is the final extension including the dot, `.log`. `parent` is `/srv/app/logs`, and its `name` is the last component, `logs`. Doing this by hand means `rsplit`, edge cases for paths without extensions, and separator rules: knowledge `pathlib` keeps inside.

questions.prompt: Your app has 40 call sites that fetch URLs, and all of them want the same retry behaviour (3 attempts, exponential backoff). Which design is better and why?
questions.code:
# Design A
def fetch(url, *, retries=3, backoff=0.5, timeout=10):
    ...

html = fetch("https://example.com")

# Design B
policy = RetryPolicy()
policy.set_max_attempts(3)
policy.set_backoff(ExponentialBackoff(base=0.5))
client = HttpClient(policy=policy, timeout=10)
html = client.fetch("https://example.com")
options: B, because separating policy, strategy and client follows the single-responsibility principle, so it is always better
A, because fewer classes always means less complexity
A, because the common case is one line with sensible defaults, while rare callers can still pass `retries=` or `backoff=`; B makes all 40 callers assemble the same objects
B, because A cannot be tested
questions.explain: A is the deeper module for this codebase: the interface cost for the common case is just `fetch(url)`, and the flexibility is still there through defaulted keyword arguments. B is shallow here: every caller repeats four lines of setup, which is change amplification waiting to happen. B is not untestable, and "fewer classes always" is too strong: B could be right if callers genuinely needed many different policies.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the **shallowest** module?
options: `json.loads(text)`, which parses any JSON document into Python objects
`hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()`
`sqlite3.connect(path)`, which opens or creates a database file
`def get_name(user): return user.name`, used in place of reading `user.name` directly
questions.explain: `get_name` has an interface (a name, a parameter) as large as its entire body, so callers learn something new and gain nothing. The others hide substantial work (a parser, a database engine, a cryptographic hash) behind one or two calls.

lessons.why: Deep modules give a lot of power through a small interface, so most of the system can ignore their details. It's the single most useful test of a design.

A simple interface hiding a lot of functionality.
An interface nearly as complex as what it does.
Splitting into many tiny classes that each add an interface but little power.

mistakes.wrong: Smaller classes and functions are always better.
mistakes.right: Many shallow pieces multiply interfaces to learn. Aim for depth, not size.

mistakes.wrong: Exposing every option makes a module flexible.
mistakes.right: Make the common case one simple call with sensible defaults; expose options only when needed.

lessons.title: Information hiding and leakage
lessons.objective: By the end you can identify where a design decision leaks across modules, including through back doors and return types, and move it behind one module's interface.
concept: **Information hiding**, described by David Parnas in 1972, means each module encapsulates a design decision, such as a file format, a data structure, or which database you use, so that the decision can change without touching other modules. The hidden knowledge is the module's *secret*. If `OrderRepository` is the only code that knows orders live in Postgres with an integer `status` column, then switching that column to an enum is a one-file change, and nobody else even has to know it happened.

**Information leakage** is the opposite: one design decision is reflected in several modules. Leakage is not always visible in an interface. If `exporter.py` writes `id|name|price` and `importer.py` splits on `|`, they are coupled even though neither imports the other: a *back-door* dependency. A common cause is **temporal decomposition**, structuring code by the order things happen (read, then parse, then write) instead of by the knowledge each part needs, so the file format ends up known by all three steps.

Leaks often travel through return values. A method that returns a raw database row or a `dict` with column names forces callers to know the schema; returning a small domain object or dataclass keeps the secret. Returning your internal list lets callers mutate your state behind your back. Getters and setters for every private field are not information hiding either: they publish the representation with extra steps. Ask of every decision: "If I changed this, how many files would I touch?" The answer should be one.

write_report() knows the format

right.title: Knowledge-based (hidden)

Callers never see delimiters or columns

example.explain: The tuple layout, the expiry check and the choice of clock are now `TTLCache`'s secrets. Switching from `time.time` to `time.monotonic` (which cannot jump backwards when the system clock changes) touched only this class, and the injectable `clock` makes expiry testable without sleeping.

lessons.tryit: Pick one design decision in your project (a date format, the database driver, the shape of an API payload, a cache key scheme) and use `rg` or your editor's search to list every file that depends on it. Count the files. Then sketch the module that would own that decision as its secret, and write the one to three methods its interface needs.

questions.prompt: What is **temporal decomposition**?
options: Caching values with an expiry time
Splitting work across threads so it runs at the same time
Organizing commits by date
Splitting a program into modules by the order in which operations happen, which tends to spread one piece of knowledge across several modules
questions.explain: Temporal decomposition structures code as read, then parse, then write. Each step needs to know the format, so the format leaks into all of them. Ousterhout recommends grouping by knowledge instead: one module that owns the format, used by whatever steps need it. The other options are unrelated uses of time.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `members()` returns the internal list itself, not a copy, so the caller's `append` mutates `Team`'s private state. The leading underscore promised privacy that the return value broke. Returning `tuple(self._members)` keeps the representation secret and makes this print 1.

questions.prompt: A `ReportService` is used by the web UI, a CSV export and an email digest. Which design is better and why?
options: They are equivalent because both return a list
A, because dataclasses cannot be serialized to CSV
A, because returning rows directly is faster and avoids an extra layer
B, because the column names and types are now the service's secret: renaming `amt` in the schema changes one file instead of three callers, and callers get real types
questions.explain: In A every caller indexes `row["amt"]` and `row["region_cd"]`, so the schema has leaked into three modules. B converts once at the boundary; the cost of building small objects is negligible next to the query. Dataclasses serialize to CSV easily with `dataclasses.astuple` or `asdict`. Both return a list, but of very different things.

questions.prompt: Which statement about these two files is most accurate?
questions.code:
# exporter.py
line = f"{p.id}|{p.name}|{p.price_cents}\n"

# importer.py  (different team, different repo folder)
pid, name, price = line.rstrip("\n").split("|")
options: The only problem is that `split` is slow
They are independent: neither imports the other, so there is no coupling
They share a back-door dependency on the line format; adding a field or a name containing `|` breaks the importer. Both directions belong in one module that owns the format
The fix is to add a comment in each file saying the other exists
questions.explain: Coupling is about shared knowledge, not imports. Both files encode the same decision (field order and delimiter), so a change to one silently breaks the other: classic leakage. A comment makes the leak visible but keeps it; putting `encode_product` and `decode_product` in one `product_format` module (or using the `csv` module, which handles quoting) removes it. Speed is not the issue.

lessons.why: When a design decision lives in one module, you can change it in one place. Leakage is why small changes turn into multi-file hunts.

terms.d: Each module encapsulates one design decision behind its interface.
One decision reflected in several modules.
Modules sharing knowledge without it appearing in any interface, like a file format.
Splitting code by the order things happen rather than by the knowledge they use.

mistakes.wrong: If two modules don't call each other, they're independent.
mistakes.right: If both know the same file format or schema, changing it breaks both. That's leakage.

mistakes.wrong: Returning raw database rows keeps things simple.
mistakes.right: It forces every caller to know the schema. Return a small domain object instead.

Look for knowledge shared through formats, ordering and return types.
Group code by the knowledge it needs, not by the order it runs.

lessons.title: Naming
lessons.objective: By the end you can rename variables and functions so they are precise, consistent and carry units, and explain what a hard-to-name thing says about the design.
concept: A name is a small piece of documentation that is read every time the code is read. Good names are **precise**, creating an accurate picture of what the thing is, and **consistent**: the same name always means the same thing, and the same thing always has the same name. `data`, `info`, `result`, `tmp` and `manager` are vague because they fit almost anything, so they tell the reader almost nothing. If you struggle to find a precise name, treat it as a design signal: the thing may be doing two jobs.

Put in the information a reader needs to avoid mistakes. A parameter called `timeout` invites `timeout=5` when the function expects milliseconds; `timeout_ms` prevents the bug. A boolean called `flag` says nothing, while `is_expired` or `has_unsaved_changes` reads like English inside an `if`. Name functions by what they return or do from the caller's point of view (`unpaid_invoices()`, `send_reminder()`), not how they work inside (`loop_and_filter()`). Skip type prefixes the reader can already see, like `str_name`.

Name length should track scope. `i` is fine in a three-line loop; a constant used across files deserves `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`. Consistency across a codebase matters more than any single perfect name: if `fetch_` means a network call and `load_` means a disk read everywhere, a new `get_user()` that hits the network breaks the reader's mental map. Renaming is one of the cheapest, safest refactorings with an editor's rename-symbol command, so do it the moment you notice a name lying to you.

rows: Reads as English inside an if

example.explain: Only names and the loop shape changed; the dict keys stay the same because they are part of the data format. A reader of the new version knows what goes in, what unit the cutoff uses, what the boolean does, and what comes out without reading the body.

lessons.tryit: Open a file you wrote at least three months ago and list ten names in it. For each, write in one line what a stranger would guess it means and what it actually means. Rename every name where the two differ using your editor's rename-symbol feature, then run the tests.

questions.prompt: Which parameter name best prevents a units bug?
options: `delay`
`delay_ms`
`delay_value`
questions.explain: `delay_ms` tells every caller the unit at the call site, so `delay_ms=5` cannot be mistaken for five seconds. `delay` and `delay_value` are equally ambiguous about units, and `d` is worse because it does not even say what the number is.

questions.prompt: The caller meant 1500 milliseconds. What does this print?
questions.explain: The function treats `timeout` as seconds, so 1500 becomes 25 minutes, and the token lives 1000 times longer than intended. Nothing in the name `timeout` warned the caller; `timeout_s` (or taking a `timedelta`) would have made the mismatch visible at the call site.

questions.prompt: Which design is better and why?
questions.code:
# Design A
def schedule(job, run_now, recurring): ...
schedule(report_job, True, False)

# Design B
class When(Enum):
    NOW = "now"
    NIGHTLY = "nightly"

def schedule(job, *, when: When): ...
schedule(report_job, when=When.NOW)
options: A, because enums add an import
A, because positional booleans keep the signature short
B, because the call site states its meaning; in A a reader cannot tell what `True, False` means without opening the definition, and swapping the two arguments is a silent bug
They are equivalent; it is purely a style preference
questions.explain: Names at the call site are where code is read most. A's boolean trap forces every reader to look up parameter order, and `schedule(job, False, True)` vs `schedule(job, True, False)` both type-check. B makes illegal mixes (both now and recurring?) harder and each call self-explanatory. An extra import is a trivial cost compared to misread calls.

questions.prompt: In your codebase every `get_*` function is an in-memory lookup and every `fetch_*` function makes a network call. A new teammate adds `get_exchange_rate()`, which calls an external API with a 10-second timeout. What is the main problem?
options: Functions should never call external APIs
The name is too long
There is no problem as long as it has a docstring
The name breaks the codebase's convention, so callers will treat it as cheap and call it in a loop or a hot path; it should be `fetch_exchange_rate()`
questions.explain: Consistent naming lets readers predict cost and behaviour from the name alone. A `get_` that blocks for up to 10 seconds will be misused by anyone who trusts the convention. A docstring helps only people who open it; the name is what everyone sees at every call site.

terms.d: Creates an accurate picture of what the thing is.
The same word always means the same thing across the codebase.
`timeout_ms`, `size_bytes`: stop unit mix-ups.
Short for tiny scopes, descriptive for wide ones.

mistakes.wrong: Short names like `d` or `tmp` keep code compact.
mistakes.right: They make every reader guess. Use short names only in tiny scopes like a three-line loop.

mistakes.wrong: Struggling to name something just means I need a thesaurus.
mistakes.right: It often means the thing does too much or isn't a clear concept. Reconsider the design.

Use one word per concept everywhere.
Treat a hard-to-name thing as a design smell.

lessons.title: Comments that explain why
lessons.objective: By the end you can delete comments that restate code, write an interface comment that lets a caller skip the body, and add implementation comments that record non-obvious reasons.
concept: Code says *what* happens. It cannot say *why* it is done this way, what was tried and rejected, or what a caller must never do. Comments exist to capture what was in the designer's head but cannot be expressed in code. A comment that restates the line below, like `i += 1  # increment i`, costs reading time and adds nothing. A comment such as `# webhooks are retried for days; dedupe on event.id or we double-charge` can prevent a production incident that no amount of clean code would have warned you about.

Ousterhout separates **interface comments** from **implementation comments**. Interface comments (docstrings) describe what a function or class does, its arguments, return value, side effects, errors and preconditions, at a higher level than the code, so callers never need to read the body. Implementation comments live inside the body and explain non-obvious reasons: a workaround, a performance choice, a subtle invariant. If the docstring for a module is hard to write briefly and clearly, the abstraction itself is probably muddled.

Comments rot when they sit far from the code they describe or narrate mechanics that change often. Keep them next to the code, at the level of intent, and update them in the same commit as the code. Link to the issue or design doc for long history (`# See #4312`). Treat "the code is self-documenting" with suspicion: good names remove the need for *what* comments, but no name can explain why `MAX_BATCH = 500` instead of 1000, or which bug a strange-looking check prevents.

left.title: Delete these
points: Restating the next line
Narrating mechanics that will change
Commented-out code (git remembers it)
Bare TODO with no reason or owner

right.title: Keep and write these
points: Docstrings: inputs, outputs, errors, side effects
Why this approach, what was rejected
Constraints from outside the code (APIs, laws, incidents)
Links to the issue or design doc

example.code:
def charge(customer_id: str, amount_cents: int, idempotency_key: str) -> Charge:
    """Charge the customer's default card.

    Safe to retry: a second call with the same idempotency_key returns the
    original Charge instead of charging again. Raises CardDeclined if the
    bank refuses. Network timeouts are retried internally and never raised.
    """
    # Backoff is capped at 8s: the provider rate-limits bursts per key, and a
    # tight retry loop got our account temporarily blocked (incident #212).
    ...
example.explain: The docstring is the interface: a caller learns the retry guarantee and which errors to handle without reading the body. The implementation comment records a reason that came from outside the code, which is exactly what a future maintainer about to "simplify" the backoff needs to know.

lessons.tryit: Take the largest function in a project you own. Delete every comment that restates the code, write a docstring that lets a caller use the function without reading its body (inputs, output, side effects, errors), and add at most two implementation comments that explain a non-obvious why. Ask a friend to call the function using only the docstring and note every question they ask.

questions.prompt: Which comment adds the most information that the code cannot express?
options: `# set retries to 3`
`# Batch size 500: the provider rejects requests over 1 MB, and 500 rows is about 0.8 MB at our max row size`
`# loop over the users`
`# TODO: improve`
questions.explain: Only the batch-size comment records a reason and a constraint invisible in the code, and tells the next person what breaks if they raise the number. The loop and retries comments restate the code. A bare TODO says something is wrong without saying what.

questions.prompt: A docstring says `Returns the user's email address.` The code returns `None` for deactivated users, and two callers crashed calling `.lower()` on the result. What is the best fix?
options: Delete the docstring, since the code is the truth
Leave it; callers should read the implementation
Add a comment at each crashing caller
Change the docstring to state that it returns `None` for deactivated users, in the same commit as a review of the callers (or change the function to raise or return a typed result)
questions.explain: An interface comment must describe everything a caller needs, and the `None` case is exactly the kind of thing that causes bugs. Fixing it at the interface helps every caller, present and future; per-caller comments repeat the knowledge (change amplification). Deleting the docstring forces every caller to read the body, which defeats the point of an interface.

questions.prompt: Which version is better and why?
options: A, because comments are always clearer than code
A, because B adds functions, and more functions mean a shallower design
They are equivalent
B, because the helper names now say what each step does, so the what-comments are unnecessary, and the one remaining comment records a reason the names cannot
questions.explain: Extracting well-named helpers turns what-comments into names the compiler keeps in sync with the code, while A's comments can drift silently. The why-comment about the 2019 data survives because no name could carry it. Extraction makes a shallow design only when helpers hide nothing; these hide real ideas behind clear names.

project.title: Deep module redesign
project.brief: Take a shallow API from one of your own projects (or a multi-step helper such as an email sender, config loader or HTTP client wrapper) and redesign it into a deep module. You will measure the interface before and after and write it up, practising every idea in this module: complexity symptoms, depth, information hiding, naming and interface comments.
milestones: Choose a module with at least three call sites; list every call site and the steps or knowledge each caller repeats.
Draw the before rectangle: count public methods, parameters and ordering rules, and mark each leaked decision and each case of change amplification.
Write the new call sites first, with the common case in one or two lines, then design an interface with defaults for the rare options.
Implement behind the new interface with docstrings, migrate every call site with tests green after each, and delete the old API.
Write a 600 to 900 word before/after report: interface counts, a diff of one call site, which secrets moved inside, and one trade-off you accepted.
project.stretch: Have someone who has never seen the code use the new module from its docstrings alone; log every question they ask and fix the interface or the comments until they ask none.

exam.prompt: This function is called from 12 places, and every caller passes the same SMTP settings from config. Which change increases depth the most?
options: Add a docstring listing all nine parameters
Rename it to `send_mail`
Make a `Mailer` that reads SMTP settings from config once, so callers write `mailer.send(to, subject, body)`
Split it into `connect()`, `login()`, `compose()` and `send()` so each step is reusable
exam.explain: The SMTP host, port, TLS flag and credentials are knowledge the module can own; callers should not have to supply it 12 times. Splitting into four calls makes the interface bigger and adds ordering rules, which is shallower. Renaming and documenting do not change the interface's size.

exam.prompt: Two modules handle the same date string. What does this print?
exam.code:
def save(d):  # d is (year, month, day); writes "DD/MM/YYYY"
    return f"{d[2]:02d}/{d[1]:02d}/{d[0]}"

def load(s):  # written by another team, who assumed "MM/DD/YYYY"
    m, d, y = s.split("/")
    return (int(y), int(m), int(d))

print(load(save((2026, 3, 7))))
exam.explain: `save` writes `07/03/2026` (day first). `load` reads the first field as the month, so 7 March becomes 3 July with no error raised. The date format is a decision known by two modules: a back-door dependency. Putting both functions in one module that owns the format, or using ISO 8601, removes the leak.

exam.prompt: According to Ousterhout, what are the two root causes of complexity?
options: Long files and long functions
Dependencies and obscurity
Too many classes and too few comments
Bugs and missing tests
exam.explain: Complexity comes from dependencies (code that cannot be understood or changed in isolation) and obscurity (important information that is not obvious). Long files, missing tests and class counts can contribute, but they are symptoms or proxies, not the root causes he identifies.

exam.prompt: A React date picker is used on 15 forms. Which component interface is better and why?
options: B, because the open/closed state and visible month are the picker's own business; A leaks them into 15 parents, each of which must wire six props correctly
B, because it renders faster
A, because lifting all state up gives the parent full control
A, because B cannot be controlled at all
exam.explain: This connects deep modules to the components you built in earlier stages. A is shallow: the interface exposes internal UI state that no parent cares about, so every form repeats the same plumbing. B is still a controlled component for the value that matters (`value`/`onChange`); it just hides the rest. Render speed is not the deciding factor.

exam.prompt: A code reviewer sees this comment above a check. What should they suggest?
exam.code:
# Payment provider rejects "UK"; ISO 3166 says "GB". Old mobile clients
# (<= 4.2) still send "UK", so normalize here rather than at the edge.
if country == "UK":
    country = "GB"
options: Replace it with a function name like `check_country_code_is_not_uk_for_legacy_reasons()`
Delete it, because comments rot
Keep it: it records a non-obvious reason and the consequence of removing the check, which no name could express
Move it to the README
exam.explain: This is exactly the kind of why-comment worth keeping: it explains a constraint from outside the code, gives the evidence, and warns what breaks. A giant function name cannot hold the history, and a README is far from the code, so it will drift.

exam.prompt: Which change is the clearest example of **strategic** programming?
options: Rewriting the whole service in a new framework
Adding a `# HACK` comment and moving on
While adding a feature, spending an extra hour to give the duplicated pricing rule a single home, so this and future features change it in one place
Copying a 40-line function to make a variant for the new endpoint
exam.explain: Strategic programming invests a modest, ongoing slice of time in design while delivering features. Copying and hacks are tactical. A full rewrite is not a small, continuous investment; it is a big risky bet, and module 2 covers why it is rarely the right call.

exam.prompt: Which interface for a rate limiter is better and why?
exam.code:
# Design A
bucket = limiter.get_bucket(user_id)
now = time.monotonic()
bucket.tokens = min(bucket.capacity, bucket.tokens + (now - bucket.last) * bucket.rate)
bucket.last = now
if bucket.tokens >= 1:
    bucket.tokens -= 1
    handle(request)

# Design B
if limiter.allow(user_id):
    handle(request)
options: B, because it uses fewer lines in the class
A, because B hides errors
B, because A leaks the bucket representation and makes every caller implement the refill rule; B keeps the algorithm secret, so switching to a sliding window later changes one class
A, because the caller can see exactly how the limiter works
exam.explain: A's callers must know the token bucket algorithm and repeat it, so the algorithm is no longer a secret, and cognitive load and change amplification follow. B's interface is a single question the caller actually cares about. Seeing how it works is not a caller's need, B hides no errors, and class line count is irrelevant to depth.

modules.summary: Change the structure of existing code without changing its behaviour: safely, in small steps, under tests, and only where it pays off.

lessons.title: Code smells and where to start
lessons.objective: By the end you can name the common code smells on sight, map each to the refactoring that fixes it, and pick refactoring targets using change frequency.
concept: Martin Fowler defines **refactoring** as changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behaviour, and a **code smell** as a surface sign that usually points to a deeper problem. A smell is a prompt to look closer, not a rule. The ones worth spotting instantly: **Long Function**, **Duplicated Code**, **Long Parameter List**, **Feature Envy** (a method that uses another object's data more than its own), **Data Clumps** (the same few fields always travelling together), **Primitive Obsession** (raw strings and ints for money, emails or statuses) and **Shotgun Surgery** (one change forces small edits in many classes).

Each smell maps to known refactorings from Fowler's catalog. Long Function leads to *Extract Function*. Data Clumps and Long Parameter List lead to *Introduce Parameter Object*. Feature Envy leads to *Move Function* into the class whose data it uses. Primitive Obsession leads to *Replace Primitive with Object*, such as a `Money` class that refuses to add dollars to euros. Shotgun Surgery is module 1's change amplification under another name; the fix is to gather the scattered knowledge into one module.

Prioritize smells by where people are working. A smelly file nobody has touched in three years costs little; the same smell in a file that changes every week costs you on every change. `git log --format= --name-only | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` lists the most frequently changed files. Combine that with a complexity measure such as `radon cc -s` for Python to find code that is both complicated and changed often. Those **hotspots** are where refactoring pays back fastest.

visual.title: Smell to refactoring
rows: You scroll to understand one function
Method mostly uses another object's fields
Money as float, status as string
One change, edits in many files
Extract Function, then call it twice

example.explain: Introduce Parameter Object gave the four fields one home, and Move Function put the formatting next to the data it uses. Any other function that took `street, city, postcode, country` can now take one `Address`.

lessons.tryit: Run the hotspot command on one of your repositories and take the top three files. In each, find three smells and write them as `smell / line range / refactoring you would apply`. Do not change any code yet; you will use this list in the module project.

questions.prompt: Which smell describes a method that reads four fields of another object and none of its own?
options: Primitive Obsession
Feature Envy
Long Parameter List
Shotgun Surgery
questions.explain: Feature Envy is a method more interested in another class's data than its own; the usual fix is Move Function to that class. Shotgun Surgery is about one change spreading over many classes, Primitive Obsession is about raw types standing in for concepts, and Long Parameter List is about the signature.

questions.prompt: Which refactoring best addresses the smell in this code?
questions.code:
def book(room, start_date, end_date, guest): ...
def price(room, start_date, end_date, coupon=None): ...
def is_available(room, start_date, end_date): ...
# each function begins with:
#   if end_date <= start_date: raise ValueError("bad range")
options: Rename `start_date` to `start`
Inline Function on `book`
Introduce Parameter Object: a `DateRange` (with `nights()` and `overlaps()`) passed instead of two loose dates
Extract Function on the body of `price`
questions.explain: `start_date` and `end_date` always travel together and every function re-validates them: a Data Clump. A `DateRange` object gives the pair one home, validates once in its constructor, and attracts the behaviour (`nights`, `overlaps`) that is currently duplicated. Extracting or inlining functions and renaming do not remove the clump.

questions.prompt: You have one day for refactoring. File A has a 600-line function, last changed in 2021. File B has an 80-line module with duplicated pricing logic and was changed in 41 commits last quarter. Which do you refactor first and why?
options: B, because refactoring pays off through future changes, and B is where changes are happening; A's cost is only paid when someone touches it
A, because old code is more likely to have bugs
Neither: refactoring should only happen in a dedicated sprint
A, because longer functions are always the worst smell
questions.explain: The value of refactoring is cheaper future changes, so it is highest where change frequency is high. B's duplication is paid for on almost every one of those 41 commits. A is ugly but dormant; refactor it when a change needs to go there. Refactoring is best done continuously, not saved for a special sprint.

questions.prompt: This `Money` type replaces raw floats (Replace Primitive with Object). What does this print?
questions.explain: `__add__` checks currencies before adding, so mixing USD and EUR raises instead of silently producing a meaningless 38.49. With raw floats, `19.99 + 18.50` would just work and be wrong. Storing cents as an int also avoids float rounding errors in money.

lessons.why: Smells point at the parts of a codebase that will cost you most. Combining them with change frequency tells you where refactoring actually pays.

terms.d: Changing internal structure without changing observable behaviour.
A surface sign of a deeper design problem, like Long Function or Duplicated Code.
One change requires small edits in many places.
A file that is both complex and frequently changed.

mistakes.wrong: Every smell should be fixed as soon as it's found.
mistakes.right: Smells in code nobody touches cost little. Prioritise hotspots that change often.

mistakes.wrong: Refactoring means rewriting code to be better.
mistakes.right: Refactoring keeps behaviour identical. Changing behaviour is a separate step.

Find hotspots with `git log` change counts.
Refactor where people are working.

lessons.title: Safe refactoring steps under tests
lessons.objective: By the end you can perform a refactoring as a series of small, separately committed, test-verified steps, including a parallel change to a widely used signature.
concept: The core discipline: never refactor and change behaviour in the same step. Kent Beck's advice is "make the change easy (warning: this may be hard), then make the easy change." A refactoring is a sequence of tiny behaviour-preserving moves, each followed by running the tests, each small enough that if the tests go red you know exactly which edit caused it and can undo it in seconds. Commit after every green step. A good refactor looks like a string of small commits, not one heroic diff.

A safe rhythm: make sure tests cover the code you are about to touch, and see them pass; make one mechanical change, such as a rename, an extracted variable or a moved function; run the tests; commit; repeat. Prefer your editor's automated refactorings (rename symbol, extract method, change signature) because they are less error-prone than hand edits. To change a widely used function signature, use **parallel change** (also called expand and contract): add the new form, migrate callers one at a time, then delete the old form.

Keep refactoring commits separate from feature commits so reviewers can check each with the right mindset: a pure refactor should not change any existing test's assertions. If you find yourself editing an assertion mid-refactor, stop. Either you changed behaviour, or the test was coupled to implementation details and needs fixing first, in its own commit. Fast tests are a precondition: if the suite takes 20 minutes you will batch many edits per run, and batching is what makes refactoring dangerous.

steps.label: Tests green
steps.detail: Run the suite before touching anything

steps.label: One small move
steps.detail: Rename, extract, move: one at a time

steps.label: Run tests
steps.detail: Red? Undo the move, do not debug it

steps.label: Repeat
steps.detail: Behaviour changes go in separate commits

example.explain: At every step the program works and the tests pass, so you can stop, ship or revert at any point. The keyword-only `team_id` and the new `role` default make call sites clearer without breaking anyone during the migration.

lessons.tryit: Pick a function in one of your projects that has at least two callers and a test. Rename it and change its signature using parallel change in at least four separate commits, running the tests before each commit. Then run `git log --oneline` and check that every commit message describes exactly one step.

questions.prompt: What is **parallel change** (expand and contract)?
options: Changing a function and all its callers in one atomic commit
Two developers refactoring the same file on different branches
Adding the new form of an interface alongside the old one, migrating callers gradually, then removing the old form
Running the test suite on several CPU cores at once
questions.explain: Parallel change keeps the system working at every step: old and new forms coexist while callers move over, and each step can be shipped or reverted on its own. A single atomic commit across all callers is the risky big-bang alternative that parallel change avoids.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps of a parallel change that replaces `invite_user(email, team_id)` with `send_invite(email, *, team_id, role)`.
lines: Add send_invite() with the new signature and its own tests
Make invite_user() a thin shim that calls send_invite()
Migrate each caller to send_invite(), running tests and committing after each
Confirm with rg "invite_user\(" that no callers remain
questions.explain: The new function must exist before the old one can delegate to it. Callers migrate while both exist, so nothing breaks mid-way. You search for remaining callers before deleting, because deleting first would break whatever you missed.

questions.prompt: Halfway through refactoring `calculate_discount`, a characterization test fails. You notice the old code had a bug: it gave 10% instead of 15% to gold members, and the test pinned the buggy 10%. What should you do?
options: Delete the failing test because it encodes a bug
Leave the test failing and mention it in the PR description
Fix the bug now and update the test, since you are already in that code
Undo your last step so the test passes again, finish the refactor preserving the 10% behaviour, then fix the bug in a separate commit with a test that asserts 15%
questions.explain: Mixing a behaviour change into a refactor means a reviewer cannot tell which diffs are safe moves and which change results. The failing test told you your step changed behaviour, so undo it. Fixing the bug later, separately, gives it its own review, its own test and its own revert if a customer depended on the old number. Deleting tests or leaving them red removes the safety net.

questions.prompt: A PR titled "Refactor pricing module" moves 400 lines into new files and, in the same commit, changes how tax is rounded. What is the best review response?
options: Ask the author to split it into a pure refactor commit or PR (no behaviour change, tests untouched) and a separate tax-rounding change with its own tests
Reject the whole PR
Approve: refactors often include small fixes
Review only the tax change and trust the moved lines
questions.explain: Moved code and changed behaviour need different kinds of review: the first is checked for exact equivalence, the second for correctness of the new rule. Mixed together, the rounding change hides among 400 moved lines. Splitting is cheap for the author and makes both reviews reliable; outright rejection or partial review are worse outcomes.

lessons.why: Small, tested refactoring steps let you improve code continuously without breaking it. Mixing refactors with feature changes is how regressions slip through.

terms.d: Refactor first so the feature becomes a small change.
One small, behaviour-preserving edit like a rename or extraction.
Add the new form, migrate callers gradually, then remove the old.
A commit that changes structure but no test assertions.

mistakes.wrong: I'll refactor and add the feature in one commit to save time.
mistakes.right: Reviewers can't tell which changes alter behaviour. Keep them in separate commits.

mistakes.wrong: Big refactors need a big branch.
mistakes.right: Use small steps and parallel change so main always works.

takeaways: Tests green, one mechanical step, tests green, commit.
Change widely used signatures with expand, migrate, contract.
Never refactor and change behaviour in the same step.

lessons.title: Characterization tests for legacy code
lessons.objective: By the end you can put untested legacy code under characterization tests that pin its current behaviour, including quirks, and introduce seams to make it testable.
concept: Michael Feathers defines **legacy code** simply as code without tests. You cannot refactor it safely because you have no way to know whether you changed behaviour, and often nobody knows what the correct behaviour is: the spec is lost, the author has left, and other systems depend on today's quirks. A **characterization test** records what the code *actually does* now, not what it should do. It is a safety net for change, not a claim of correctness.

The recipe: call the code with a realistic input, write an assertion you know is wrong (`assert result == "?"`), run it, and copy the actual value from the failure message into the assertion. Repeat with inputs chosen to hit each branch: empty input, boundary values, odd casing, error paths. For large outputs such as reports or HTML, a **golden master** (snapshot) test saves the whole output to a file and diffs against it. `pytest --cov --cov-branch` shows which branches still have no test under them.

To get code under test you may need a **seam**: a place where you can change behaviour without editing the code at that spot. In Python the cheapest seams are parameters with defaults, such as `def digest(now=None): now = now or datetime.now()`, and injecting clocks, random sources, database handles and HTTP clients. When a characterization test reveals something that looks like a bug, do not fix it in the same step. Pin it, add a comment like `# BUG? lowercase country codes get international rates, see #88`, and fix it later as a deliberate change.

example.explain: Each test was written by asserting a wrong value and copying the real one from the failure. The third test pins a likely bug so the refactor cannot change it by accident; fixing it later will be a separate, reviewed behaviour change.

lessons.tryit: Take an untested function from an old project (or the `shipping` function in the example). Write characterization tests with the assert-wrong-then-copy technique until branch coverage reports every branch taken. Record anything that looks like a bug as a comment in the test, and do not fix it.

questions.prompt: What does a characterization test assert?
options: What the code actually does today, whether or not that is correct
That the code meets a performance budget
That the code runs without raising exceptions
What the specification says the code should do
questions.explain: Characterization tests pin current behaviour so that refactoring cannot change it unnoticed. They deliberately include quirks and suspected bugs, because other code may depend on them. A spec-based test is a normal unit test, and "does not raise" pins far too little to protect a refactor.

questions.prompt: You are characterizing this legacy function. What does the last line print?
questions.explain: At 20 kg the surcharge does not apply because the check is `> 20`, so the cost is 8 + 30.0 = 38.0. At 21 kg it is (8 + 31.5) x 1.1 = 43.45 after rounding. This boundary is exactly what characterization tests should pin: a refactor that changed `>` to `>=` would alter 20 kg prices silently.

questions.prompt: You want characterization tests for this function, but it reads the clock and the database directly. Which change is the safest seam to introduce first?
options: Mock `datetime` globally with a library that patches the standard library
Run the tests only on Mondays at 9am
Add parameters with defaults, `def send_digest(users=None, now=None, mailer=None)`, that fall back to today's behaviour, so production calls are unchanged and tests pass in fixed values
Rewrite the function to use a new DigestService class before writing any tests
questions.explain: Defaulted parameters are a tiny, mechanical change that keeps every existing call working while giving tests full control of time, data and side effects. Global patching works but is brittle and hides the dependency. Rewriting before having tests is exactly the unsafe refactor the tests are meant to protect.

questions.prompt: When is a golden master (snapshot) test the best choice?
options: When the function returns a single boolean
When the output contains the current timestamp and a random ID
When the code produces a large output, such as a 300-line HTML invoice, and you need to detect any change in it during a refactor
When you want to document the intended behaviour for new developers
questions.explain: Snapshots shine when the output is large and asserting each field by hand would take hours. A boolean needs a plain assertion. Snapshots document current behaviour, not intent. Output with timestamps or random IDs changes every run, so you must first introduce seams to fix those values or the snapshot will always fail.

lessons.why: Most code you'll change in your career has no tests. Characterization tests make it safe to touch without first understanding every line.

terms.d: Code without tests.
A test that records what the code does now, quirks included.
Saved output for many inputs, compared on every run.
A place to change behaviour without editing code there, like a parameter or injected dependency.

mistakes.wrong: Characterization tests should assert what the code ought to do.
mistakes.right: They pin what it actually does. Fix bugs later, deliberately, in a separate step.

mistakes.right: Introduce a small seam, such as a parameter with a default, then test.

lessons.title: Extracting functions and classes
lessons.objective: By the end you can apply Extract Function and Extract Class mechanically and safely, and decide when the opposite move, Inline Function, is better.
concept: **Extract Function** is the most used refactoring. Fowler's heuristic: if you have to spend effort working out what a fragment does, extract it into a function named after *what* it does, even if it is only one line. The mechanics: create the function, copy the fragment in, pass every variable it reads as a parameter, return every variable it changes that is used afterwards, replace the fragment with a call, and run the tests. If the fragment changes three locals that are used later, the extraction boundary is probably wrong.

**Extract Class** applies when one class has grown two responsibilities: a subset of fields and methods that change together and are used together. Signs include fields with a shared prefix (`billing_street`, `billing_city`, `billing_zip`), methods that only touch that subset, and a test file where half the tests set up one cluster of fields. Create the new class, move the fields first, then move the methods one at a time, leaving a delegating method on the old class until every caller has moved.

Extraction is not free: each new function is another interface to learn, and module 1 warned about shallow modules. Extract when the new function hides a real idea behind a good name, like `is_business_day(date)`, not to hit a line-count rule. The reverse refactoring, **Inline Function**, is just as legitimate when a function's body is as clear as its name, or when a chain of one-call helpers (`total()` calls `compute_total()` calls `_total_impl()`) makes readers jump through files for nothing.

left.title: Extract Function
points: Trigger: a fragment needs effort to understand
Pass in what it reads
Return what it changes
Name it for what, not how

right.title: Extract Class
points: Trigger: a subset of fields and methods change together
Shared prefixes are a tell
Move fields first, then methods
Delegate from the old class until callers migrate

example.explain: The rule for what counts as billable now has a name and one home, so the dashboard and the invoice export can reuse it instead of copying the condition. Each extraction was one step with a test run in between.

lessons.tryit: Find a function over 40 lines in your own code. Extract at least three functions using your editor's Extract Method command, running the tests after each. For each extraction write one sentence on whether the name made the calling code clearer; inline any that did not.

questions.prompt: What is Fowler's main heuristic for when to use Extract Function?
options: When you have to spend effort figuring out what a fragment of code does, so you can name it after what it does
Whenever a function has a loop
When a fragment is used exactly once
When a function is longer than 10 lines
questions.explain: Fowler's rule is about the gap between intention and implementation: if reading the fragment takes effort, a name will save every future reader that effort. Line limits are a crude proxy, and fragments used once are often still worth extracting if a name clarifies them.

questions.prompt: A developer extracted the coupon logic into its own function. What does this print?
questions.explain: Rebinding `total` inside `apply_coupon` changes only the local name; the function returns `None`, and `checkout` still returns its own unchanged `total`. The extraction forgot the rule "return every variable you modify that is used afterwards". The fix is `return total` in the helper and `total = apply_coupon(total, code)` at the call site. A test run after the extraction would have caught it.

questions.prompt: This class has grown. Which refactoring is the best next step?
questions.code:
class User:
    name: str
    email: str
    billing_street: str
    billing_city: str
    billing_zip: str
    card_last4: str
    card_expiry: str

    def billing_address_label(self): ...
    def card_is_expired(self, today): ...
    def update_card(self, last4, expiry): ...
options: Split `User` into seven classes, one per field
Extract Class: move the billing fields and their methods into a `BillingProfile` class that `User` holds, with delegating methods on `User` until callers migrate
Rename `User` to `UserManager`
Inline every method into its callers
questions.explain: The billing fields share a prefix, change together, and are used only by billing methods: the textbook sign for Extract Class. One class per field is classitis, giving many shallow interfaces. Inlining spreads billing knowledge to every caller, and the `Manager` rename makes the name vaguer without changing structure.

questions.prompt: Which version is better and why?
options: B, because A's helpers are pass-through layers that hide nothing; each adds an interface and a jump without adding meaning, so Inline Function makes the code simpler
B, because fewer lines always run faster
A, because B cannot be unit tested
A, because more functions always mean better separation of concerns
questions.explain: Each helper in A has an interface as large as its body, which is the definition of a shallow module. Inlining them leaves one clear function that is just as testable. Function count is not a measure of good design, and performance is not the issue here.

lessons.why: Extract Function and Extract Class are the refactorings you'll use most. Knowing when the reverse is better keeps you from fragmenting code into shallow pieces.

terms.d: Move a fragment into a function named after what it does.
Split a class whose fields and methods form two responsibilities.
Replace a call with the function's body when the indirection adds nothing.
A name describing what, not how.

mistakes.wrong: Extracting more functions always improves code.
mistakes.right: Each one is another interface. Extract when it hides a real idea behind a clear name.

mistakes.wrong: Extraction is a manual cut and paste.
mistakes.right: Use the editor's automated refactoring, then run the tests.

Extract a class when a subset of fields and methods change together.
Inline when a function's name says no more than its body.

lessons.title: When not to refactor
lessons.objective: By the end you can decide whether to refactor now, later or never using change frequency, test coverage and ownership, and choose the strangler fig pattern over a rewrite.
concept: Refactoring is an economic decision: you pay now to make future changes cheaper. If no future changes are coming, there is no payoff. Code that works, is not changing and is not blocking anyone, such as a stable CSV exporter or a finished migration script, can stay ugly. Fowler suggests refactoring code you are about to change (**preparatory refactoring**, so the change becomes easy) and code you just struggled to understand (**comprehension refactoring**, so the next reader does not struggle), and leaving the rest alone.

Some moments are wrong for refactoring. Without a safety net, and with no way to add characterization tests, only small automated editor refactorings are safe. Right before a release freeze or in the middle of an incident, stability beats tidiness. In code you do not own, especially open source, an unrequested 2,000-line cleanup is usually closed unread however good it is. And be wary of the **big rewrite**: Joel Spolsky's essay on Netscape argues that throwing away working code throws away years of bug fixes hidden in its ugliness.

When a module really is beyond saving, use the **strangler fig** pattern: put new behaviour behind the same interface in a new implementation, route traffic to it piece by piece (often with a feature flag), and delete the old code once nothing reaches it. Every step ships and can be rolled back. Finally, write the decision down. A short note in the PR or an architecture decision record saying "we chose not to refactor X because Y" stops the next person from reopening the same debate.

questions.prompt: What is **preparatory refactoring**?
options: Refactoring in a separate branch that is never merged
Writing a design document before refactoring
Refactoring every file before starting a new project
Restructuring code you are about to change so that the upcoming change becomes easy
questions.explain: Preparatory refactoring is the "make the change easy, then make the easy change" move: the refactoring is justified by the change you are about to make. Refactoring everything up front has no specific payoff, and an unmerged branch helps nobody.

questions.prompt: Which piece of code is the best candidate to refactor **now**?
options: A one-off script that migrated data last year and will never run again
The order validation module, which you must modify this week to add a new country, and which has decent tests but duplicated rules for each country
A 900-line report generator that has not changed in two years and has no open issues
A vendored copy of a third-party library
questions.explain: Validation is about to change, has a safety net, and contains duplication the new country would make worse, so refactoring first makes this week's change easier. The report generator is ugly but dormant. Vendored code should be updated from upstream, not reshaped locally, and a dead script has no future changes to make cheaper.

questions.prompt: Your team proposes rewriting an 8-year-old billing service from scratch over six months, freezing new features meanwhile. Which plan is better and why?
options: The rewrite, because a clean codebase is worth six months
Strangler fig: route one billing flow at a time to a new implementation behind the existing interface, verified against the old one, so value ships continuously and each step can be rolled back
The rewrite, but in a new language so the team learns something
Do nothing, because legacy code should never be changed
questions.explain: The old service encodes years of edge cases that no spec captures; a rewrite tends to rediscover them as production bugs, while delivering nothing for six months. Strangling migrates incrementally with a working system at every step, and characterization tests can compare old and new outputs. Doing nothing ignores real costs if the service changes often.

questions.prompt: You are fixing a one-line typo in an error message in an open-source project you have never contributed to. The surrounding module is messy. What is the best approach?
options: Fork the project and maintain your cleaned-up version
Submit the one-line fix as its own small PR; if you think the module needs a cleanup, open an issue proposing it and wait for maintainers to agree
Fix the typo and also reformat and restructure the whole module in the same PR, since you are there anyway
Skip the typo and submit only the cleanup
questions.explain: Maintainers merge small, focused PRs that are cheap to review. A drive-by restructuring of code you do not own is costly to review, risks merge conflicts with their work, and usually gets closed, taking your typo fix with it. Proposing the cleanup in an issue respects their ownership; module 3 covers this workflow.

project.title: Refactor an old project under characterization tests
project.brief: Take a project of yours that is at least six months old and that you would like to extend, put its hotspots under characterization tests, and refactor them in small verified steps. You will practise smell detection, test-first safety nets, extraction and the judgement of what to leave alone.
milestones: Pick the project and run the hotspot and complexity commands (`git log` frequency plus `radon cc` or similar) to choose two or three target files; record their baseline metrics.
Write characterization tests until branch coverage on the target files is at least 80%, recording coverage before and after; pin suspected bugs with comments instead of fixing them.
Refactor in at least 15 small commits, each with green tests and a message naming the refactoring used (Extract Function, Introduce Parameter Object, Move Function and so on).
Keep a log of every smell found, the refactoring applied, and anything you deliberately left alone with the reason.
Add one new feature after the refactor and compare the number of files you actually touched with your estimate for the pre-refactor code.
Write a one-page report with before/after metrics: longest function, average cyclomatic complexity, coverage, and the commit list.
project.stretch: Fix one of the pinned bugs as a deliberate, separately reviewed behaviour change: update its characterization test, search for anything that depended on the old behaviour, and document the change in a changelog entry.

exam.prompt: Which smell is most prominent here?
options: Long Parameter List
Data Clumps
Feature Envy
Primitive Obsession: statuses are bare strings, so typos like "canceled" vs "cancelled" are possible and every rule about statuses is scattered
exam.explain: Order status is a domain concept represented as raw strings compared in several places. A typo silently creates a new status, and the set of valid transitions has no home. Replace Primitive with Object (an `Enum`, or a class with transition rules) fixes it. There is no long parameter list, no clump of fields, and no method envying another object here.

exam.prompt: You are writing characterization tests for this legacy function. What exact value should the pinned assertion contain for the printed expression?
exam.explain: 9 is divisible by 3 only, 10 by 5 only, 30 by 15 (checked first, so it never reaches the 3 or 5 branches), and 7 falls through to `str(7)`, which is the string `'7'`, not the int 7. Pinning one input per branch like this is how characterization tests reach full branch coverage.

exam.prompt: In this module's terms, **Shotgun Surgery** is the same problem module 1 called:
options: Deep modules
Change amplification
Cognitive load
Information hiding
exam.explain: Shotgun Surgery means one logical change requires many small edits across the codebase, which is exactly change amplification. Both are fixed the same way: gather the scattered knowledge into one module. Information hiding and deep modules are the cures, not the problem.

exam.prompt: You must refactor a function with no tests that calls `random.random()` and `time.time()`. Which first step is safest?
options: Refactor carefully by hand and test manually in the browser
Write the new version first, then write tests for the new version
Delete the randomness since it makes testing hard
Introduce seams by adding defaulted parameters (`rng=random.random, clock=time.time`), then write characterization tests with fixed values, then refactor
exam.explain: Seams make the non-deterministic inputs controllable without changing production behaviour, and characterization tests then pin current outputs. Manual checking is not a safety net for a refactor. Tests written for the new version cannot tell you whether it matches the old one. Deleting randomness is a behaviour change.

exam.prompt: Arrange the lines to extract the billable-revenue calculation into its own function.
exam.explain: The accumulator must be initialized before the loop, the condition sits inside the loop, the addition inside the condition, and the return comes after the loop at function level. Putting `return total` before the loop would always return 0.

exam.prompt: Which plan best fits Fowler's guidance for this situation? A module you need to change today is hard to follow, has good tests, and the feature needs a new branch in a 120-line function.
options: Add the new branch to the 120-line function now and refactor someday
Rewrite the module from scratch before adding the feature
Add the feature and the refactoring together in one commit to save time
First, in separate commits, extract the existing branches into named functions with tests green after each; then add the new branch as one more small function in a feature commit
exam.explain: This is preparatory refactoring: make the change easy, then make the easy change, with refactor commits separate from the behaviour change. Postponing makes the function worse, a rewrite is far riskier than extraction with tests available, and one mixed commit makes review and revert harder.

exam.prompt: Which is the clearest sign that a class needs **Extract Class**?
options: It has a long name
It has more than 200 lines
Several fields share a prefix (`shipping_street`, `shipping_city`, `shipping_zip`), and a group of methods uses only those fields
It inherits from another class
exam.explain: Fields with a shared prefix used by their own subset of methods are a hidden class waiting to be named. Line count is a weak proxy: a long class can be cohesive. Inheritance and name length say nothing about whether it has two responsibilities.

modules.summary: Find your way around large unfamiliar codebases and turn that skill into merged open-source contributions with clear commits, descriptions and reviews.

lessons.title: Navigating a large codebase
lessons.objective: By the end you can find where a behaviour is implemented in an unfamiliar repository using search, definition jumps, a written call chain and git history, in under an hour.
concept: Professionals spend far more time reading code than writing it, and in an unfamiliar codebase the skill is not reading every file but finding the small part that matters for your question. Start from the outside: the README, the contributing guide, the directory layout, the build file (`pyproject.toml`, `package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod`) and the entry points (`main`, CLI definitions, route tables). Then run the tests. A passing suite is an executable map of what the code is supposed to do, and it proves your setup works.

Search beats browsing. `rg -n "def resolve_" -t py` (ripgrep) finds definitions in seconds even in million-line repos, and `rg -l SessionMiddleware` lists every file that mentions a symbol. **ctags** (`ctags -R .`) builds an index so your editor can jump to any definition; editors with a language server do the same through Go to Definition and Find All References. Use them to build a **call graph** of the path you care about and write it down as a chain, such as `cli.main -> Runner.run -> Scheduler.tick -> Job.execute`.

History explains what code cannot. `git log --oneline -- path/to/file` shows how a file evolved. `git log -S "retry_after"` (the pickaxe) finds commits that added or removed that string. `git blame -w -C file` shows the last commit to touch each line, ignoring whitespace and following code moved between files. Open that commit and its pull request: the description and review discussion often contain the *why* that comments lack. Treat blame as a research tool for finding context, never as a way to find someone to blame.

example.code:
# Where is --dry-run handled in an unfamiliar Python project?
rg -n -e "--dry-run" -t py              # where the flag is defined
rg -n "dry_run" -t py | head            # follow the variable it sets
git log --oneline -S "dry_run" | tail -1  # oldest match: the commit that introduced it
git show --stat <sha>                     # what else changed with it
git blame -w -L 120,140 src/tool/cli.py   # last change to each of these lines
example.explain: `-e` is needed because the pattern starts with dashes and would otherwise be read as an option. `git log` lists newest first, so `tail -1` gives the oldest commit that touched the string. Each command answers one question and points to the next.

lessons.tryit: Clone a mid-sized project you use, such as `pallets/flask`, `psf/requests` or `httpie/cli`. Pick one user-visible behaviour (a CLI flag, an error message, a default header) and, within 45 minutes, write down the call chain from the entry point to the line that implements it, plus the commit that introduced it. Note which tool found each link.

questions.prompt: What does `git log -S "retry_after"` show?
options: Commits signed with a GPG key
Commits whose message contains `retry_after`
Every line currently containing `retry_after`
Commits that changed the number of occurrences of the string `retry_after` in the code, that is, added or removed it
questions.explain: `-S` is the pickaxe: it searches diffs for changes in how many times a string appears, which finds the commit that introduced or deleted it. Searching messages is `--grep`. Finding current lines is `rg` or `git grep`. Signature checking is `--show-signature`.

questions.prompt: You want to know why `timeout = 7` was chosen in `client.py`. What is the most direct first step?
options: Change it to 10 and see what breaks
Run `git blame -L <line>,<line> client.py`, then `git show` the commit and read its message and linked pull request
Search Stack Overflow for "timeout 7"
Ask in the project chat who wrote it
questions.explain: Blame on that exact line points to the commit that last set it, and the commit message or PR discussion usually records the reason. Asking people costs their time and may reach nobody who remembers. Changing the value is an experiment with unknown consequences, not research.

questions.prompt: You need to fix a bug in a 400,000-line repository you have never seen, and you have an afternoon. The bug produces the error message `Invalid range header`. Which strategy is best?
options: Rewrite the range-header handling from scratch based on the RFC
Reproduce the bug, `rg` for the exact error message, follow references up the call chain to the request handler, and read the tests for that function
Read every file in the `src/http/` directory alphabetically
Read the code top-down starting from `main` until you reach the relevant part
questions.explain: The error text is a unique string that leads straight to where it is raised; from there you trace callers only as far as you need. Top-down or alphabetical reading spends the afternoon on irrelevant code. A rewrite skips understanding the existing behaviour, which is the whole point of the investigation.

questions.prompt: `git blame` says the line you are investigating was last changed by a commit titled "Reformat codebase with black". What should you do next?
options: Rerun blame with `--ignore-rev <sha>` (or a `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file) so git looks past the formatting commit to the one that wrote the logic
Conclude that the formatting commit introduced the logic
Use `git log -S` with the commit hash
Give up on blame; it cannot see past reformatting
questions.explain: A mass reformat touches every line without changing meaning, hiding the real author. `--ignore-rev` tells blame to skip that commit and attribute lines to the previous change, and many projects ship a `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file listing such commits. `-w` only ignores whitespace changes, which is not enough when a formatter also changes quotes or line breaks.

lessons.title: Reading CPython- and Redis-style source
lessons.objective: By the end you can locate the implementation of a familiar built-in in a mature C codebase, read it using the project's conventions, and explain one non-obvious design choice it makes.
concept: Mature C codebases like CPython and Redis are excellent reading: they are well structured, heavily reviewed, and implement behaviour you already know from the outside. You know what `list.append` does; reading `Objects/listobject.c` shows you how. Pick something observable, find its implementation, and read just enough to explain one surprising fact. For example, `append` is amortized O(1) because `list_resize` over-allocates, so most appends find spare capacity and do not need to reallocate and copy the array.

Learn the project's conventions first, because they repeat everywhere. In CPython, public C API functions are named like `PyList_Append`; every object begins with a `PyObject` header holding a reference count and a type pointer; `Py_INCREF` and `Py_DECREF` manage lifetimes; and a function that returns `NULL` instead of an object is signalling that an exception has been set. In Redis, each command is a C function such as `setCommand(client *c)`, data types live in files like `t_string.c`, `t_list.c` and `t_hash.c`, and the event loop is in `ae.c`.

Read actively. Keep a notes file with the question you are answering, the call chain you found, and open questions. Run the code: building CPython from source (`./configure --with-pydebug && make -j8`) takes a few minutes and lets you add a `printf` or set a breakpoint and watch your Python snippet execute. Read the tests next to the code, such as `Lib/test/test_list.py`, to see which edge cases the authors cared about. Stop when you have answered your question; the goal is faster understanding, not reading everything.
