example.code:
import sys

lst, last = [], sys.getsizeof([])
for i in range(30):
    lst.append(i)
    size = sys.getsizeof(lst)
    if size != last:
        print(f"len={len(lst):2d}  bytes={size}")
        last = size
example.explain: The size jumps only at certain lengths, not on every append: those are the moments `list_resize` asks for more capacity than it needs right now. The exact numbers vary between Python versions and platforms, which is why you read the C source for your version to explain them.

lessons.tryit: Open `Objects/listobject.c` in the CPython repository and find `list_resize`. Write a 150-word explanation of its growth formula and why it makes `append` amortized O(1). Then run the example below and check that the lengths where the size jumps match your reading of the formula for your Python version.

questions.prompt: In CPython's C API, a function that normally returns a `PyObject *` returns `NULL`. What does that conventionally mean?
options: The object was garbage collected
The Python value is `None`
The function has not finished yet
An error occurred and an exception has been set, which the caller must propagate or handle
questions.explain: `NULL` is the C API's error signal: the callee has set an exception, and callers usually return `NULL` too until the interpreter raises it in Python. `None` is a real object (`Py_None`) and is returned as a non-NULL pointer, which is the classic confusion.

questions.prompt: Where in the Redis source tree would you start looking for the implementation of the `HSET` command?
options: `t_string.c`
`ae.c`
`server.h` only
`t_hash.c`
questions.explain: Redis groups command implementations by data type in `t_<type>.c` files, so hash commands like `HSET` are in `t_hash.c`. `ae.c` is the event loop, `t_string.c` holds string commands like `SET`, and headers declare functions without implementing them.

questions.prompt: You have two hours to understand how CPython's `dict` keeps insertion order. Which plan is best?
options: Watch a video about hash tables in general

Write down the question, read the comment block at the top of `dictobject.c` that describes the layout, locate the insert and iteration functions, confirm your understanding with a small experiment, and record the call chain in notes
Read `Objects/dictobject.c` from line 1 to the end
Read the entire `Python/` directory first to understand the interpreter
questions.explain: Active, question-driven reading goes straight to the relevant structures and verifies the model by experiment. `dictobject.c` is thousands of lines, so reading linearly wastes most of the time. The interpreter loop in `Python/` is irrelevant to dict layout, and a generic hash-table video will not explain CPython's compact split between an index table and an entries array.

Reading with a question, notes and the ability to run the code.
The reason a non-obvious implementation choice was made.

lessons.title: The contribution workflow
lessons.objective: By the end you can take an open-source issue from claim to opened pull request using the fork, branch, sync and PR workflow, following the project's own norms.
concept: A first open-source contribution is mostly social, not technical. Maintainers are often volunteers with little time, so your job is to make your pull request cheap to review. Start with a project you actually use. Read `CONTRIBUTING.md`, the code of conduct, and a few recently merged PRs to learn the norms: commit style, test expectations, whether an issue is required first. **Good First Issue** (goodfirstissue.dev) and labels like `good first issue` or `help wanted` point to tasks maintainers have already agreed they want.

Claim before you code. Comment on the issue with your plan ("I'd like to take this; I'm planning to X, does that sound right?") and wait for a reply; this avoids duplicate work and wrong approaches. The mechanics: **fork** on GitHub, clone your fork, add the original as the `upstream` remote, create one branch per change, make the smallest change that solves the issue plus a test, run the project's linters and tests locally, push to your fork, and open the PR against upstream, linking the issue with `Fixes #123`.

Before pushing, sync with upstream (`git fetch upstream` then `git rebase upstream/main`, or whatever the default branch is) so your branch applies cleanly. After opening, expect CI failures and review comments: reply to every comment, push fixes as new commits unless the project asks you to squash, and re-request review. If a PR goes quiet for a couple of weeks, one polite ping is fine. Small first PRs, such as a docs fix, a failing test for a reported bug or a one-function fix, get merged; large unrequested features from strangers rarely do.

example.code:
gh repo fork pallets/click --clone      # fork + clone + adds the 'upstream' remote
cd click
git switch -c fix-help-wrap-zero-width   # one branch per change
# ...edit code, add a test that failed before the fix...
pytest -q
pre-commit run --all-files               # same lint rules CI will run
git commit -am "Fix help text wrapping when terminal width is 0"
git fetch upstream
git rebase upstream/main                 # use the project's default branch
git push -u origin fix-help-wrap-zero-width
gh pr create --fill                      # then edit the description properly
example.explain: The `gh` CLI handles fork-and-clone in one step. Running tests and pre-commit locally means CI is a formality rather than a round trip, and rebasing on upstream just before pushing keeps the diff limited to your change.

questions.prompt: In the fork workflow, what is the `upstream` remote?
options: Your fork on GitHub
The CI server
A backup of your local branch
The original repository you forked from, used to fetch the latest changes
questions.explain: By convention `origin` is your fork (where you push) and `upstream` is the original project (where you fetch new commits and where your PR is merged). Mixing them up leads to pushing to the wrong place or rebasing on a stale base.

questions.prompt: Arrange the commands for a first documentation-fix contribution, from forking to opening the PR.

questions.prompt: You found a bug in a library, and fixing it properly requires changing the signature of a public function. What is the best first step?
options: Open an issue describing the bug with a minimal reproduction and your proposed fix, including the API change, and ask the maintainers whether they want it before writing the PR
Change the signature but keep it secret in the docs
Implement the change and open a large PR so maintainers can see it works
Fork the library and publish your fixed version under a new name
questions.explain: Public API changes affect every user, so maintainers need to agree on the design before code exists. An issue with a reproduction costs little and may surface a better fix or a compatibility plan. A big unrequested PR risks wasted work if they want a different approach, and a permanent fork splits the community.

questions.prompt: Your PR has green CI, you addressed all comments, and it has had no response for three weeks. What is the best action?
options: Merge it yourself using your fork
Leave one short, polite comment asking if anything else is needed, and check the project's contributing guide for a preferred way to request review
Mention every maintainer by name every day until someone replies
Close it and open an identical new PR to bump it to the top

lessons.title: Commit messages and PR descriptions
lessons.objective: By the end you can write commit messages that follow the standard conventions and PR descriptions that give a reviewer the problem, approach, risks and testing in under a minute.
concept: A commit message is a letter to a future maintainer reading `git log` or `git blame`, possibly during an outage. The widely used conventions, summarized in Chris Beams' seven rules: a subject line of about 50 characters, in the imperative mood ("Fix race in session cleanup", not "Fixed" or "fixes stuff"), capitalized, with no trailing period; a blank line; then a body wrapped at 72 characters explaining **what** changed and **why**, not how, since the diff shows how. Test the subject by completing: "If applied, this commit will ___".

Each commit should be one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own; that keeps `git bisect` and `git revert` useful, as module 5 will show. Some projects use **Conventional Commits** (`fix(parser): handle empty input`, `feat: add --json flag`) so tools can generate changelogs; follow whatever the project already does. Reference issues in the body (`Fixes #412`). Before review, clean up "WIP" and "oops" commits with an interactive rebase on your own branch unless the project squashes on merge.

A PR description is written for a reviewer who has none of your context. Google's review guide recommends a short first-line summary followed by a body that covers the problem, the approach and why it beat the alternatives, anything risky the reviewer should look at closely, how it was tested, and known follow-up work. Add screenshots for UI changes and before/after numbers for performance changes. Write it so it still makes sense a year from now, because it will be found again through blame and linked issues.

questions.prompt: A feature took you a week. Which commit history makes `git bisect` and `git revert` most useful later?

A series of commits where each is one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own, such as adding the table, then the API, then the UI
One commit per hour of work, whatever state the code was in

lessons.title: Code review: giving and receiving
lessons.objective: By the end you can review a pull request in priority order with comments that are specific, kind and labelled by severity, and respond to review on your own work without defensiveness.
concept: Code review exists to keep the codebase healthy over time and to spread knowledge, not to prove who is cleverest. Google's guideline: approve a change once it *definitely improves* the overall health of the code, even if it is not perfect. Review in priority order: design (does this belong here, is the module deep?), correctness and edge cases, tests, complexity, naming, comments, and only then style, which a formatter or linter should handle anyway. Reading the tests first is a good habit, since they show what the author believes the code does.

Write comments that are kind, specific and actionable. Comment on the code, not the person: "this loop re-reads the file for each row" rather than "you made this slow". Explain why, and suggest a fix when you can. Label severity so the author knows what blocks merging: `nit:` for optional polish, `question:` when you genuinely do not understand, and plain comments for issues that must be fixed. Ask questions when you might be missing context, and point out genuinely good decisions too; praise teaches as much as criticism.

When receiving review, assume good intent: the reviewer is spending their time to help you. Respond to every comment, either by fixing it or by explaining why not and letting them decide. If a reviewer was confused, that is data: the code or a comment probably needs to change, not just your reply in the thread. After two rounds of back-and-forth on one point, switch to a quick call. Keep PRs small, a few hundred lines at most, because reviewers find far fewer problems in large diffs.

questions.prompt: By Google's code review guidelines, when should a reviewer approve a change?

When it definitely improves the overall code health, even if it is not perfect
Only when the code is perfect
When the CI build is green, regardless of design

questions.prompt: Which review comment is most useful?

`load_tax_table() parses a 2 MB CSV and runs once per line item; invoices can have 500+ items. Could we load it once before the loop? Blocking: this caused the timeout in #377.`
`nit: I would have written this differently.`
`Why would you do it like this??`
questions.explain: It names the exact problem, the evidence, a concrete fix and the severity, and talks about the code rather than the author. The others are either unspecific, so the author cannot act, or aimed at the person. A nit with no suggestion gives nothing to act on.

questions.prompt: A reviewer asks: "Why not just use a dict here instead of this custom class?" You chose the class because it validates that `quantity` is positive. What is the best response?
options: Explain the validation reason in the thread and also add a short docstring or comment to the class, since the question shows future readers will wonder the same thing
Reply "because it's better" and resolve the thread
Ignore the comment, since it is only a question
Switch to a dict to avoid conflict

questions.prompt: You have 20 minutes to review a 350-line PR. How should you spend them?

On design and correctness first (does this belong here, what happens on empty input, errors, concurrency), then whether the tests cover those cases; leave style to the linter
On rewriting the code your way in a suggestion
On formatting and spacing, since those are quickest to spot
questions.explain: Problems in design and correctness are the expensive ones to fix later and the ones tools cannot catch. Formatting is cheap and automatable. Reading only the description skips the code, and rewriting it your way replaces review with authorship.

`Parser/`

Submit the bug fix as a small PR with a test; separately open an issue proposing the refactor with a short rationale, and do it only if maintainers agree
Do only the refactor, since it makes the bug fix easier
Do both in one PR so maintainers see the full improvement

The small fix is easy to merge; the refactor needs the owners' buy-in. Bundling or hiding the refactor makes the fix harder to review and less likely to land.

exam.prompt: A reviewer comments on your PR: "nit: maybe `retries` instead of `n`?" and "This swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` because of the bare `except:`." How should you respond?

The nit is optional, but cheap improvements are usually worth taking, and replying to every comment keeps the reviewer informed. Treating a bug as style, or silently resolving threads, wastes the review.

Read the whole repository first
Edit it immediately and rely on CI to catch problems

modules.title: A second language & paradigm
modules.summary: Pick up functional thinking, Rust's ownership model and Go's concurrency, and use error handling and types as deliberate design tools.

lessons.title: Functional ideas: purity, immutability, map/filter/reduce
lessons.objective: By the end you can separate pure logic from side effects, use immutable data to avoid aliasing bugs, and express loops as map, filter and reduce.
concept: A **pure function** returns a value that depends only on its arguments and has no side effects: it does not mutate its inputs, perform I/O, read the clock, or touch globals. `def total(prices): return sum(prices)` is pure; a function that appends to a global list or calls `datetime.now()` is not. Pure functions are easy to test (no setup, no mocks), safe to cache, safe to run in parallel, and easy to reason about, because any call can be replaced by its result without changing the program.

**Immutability** means values never change after they are created; you build new values instead. In Python, prefer tuples, `frozenset` and `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, and use `dataclasses.replace(order, status="paid")` to get a modified copy. This removes a whole class of bugs where one part of the program mutates data another part is still using. Many teams adopt **functional core, imperative shell**: keep business logic pure and immutable in the core, and push I/O such as databases, HTTP and the clock out to a thin outer layer.

**map**, **filter** and **reduce** express loops as transformations of whole collections. map applies a function to every element, filter keeps the elements that match a predicate, and reduce folds a collection into one value using a combining function and a starting value. In Python, comprehensions are the idiomatic map and filter (`[p.price for p in items if p.in_stock]`), and `sum`, `max`, `any` and `all` cover most reductions; reach for `functools.reduce` only when no built-in fits. Rust and JavaScript chain methods instead: `.iter().filter(..).map(..).sum()`.

nums = [3, 1, 4]
acc = 0
for n in nums:

print(acc)

example.explain: `apply_discount` never changes the original item, so `cart` still totals 1900 after building `sale`. Both functions are trivially testable, and because `Item` is frozen, no other code can mutate a price behind your back.

lessons.tryit: Take a function from your full-stack project that mixes logic and I/O, for example one that queries the database, computes something and sends an email. Split it into a pure function that takes plain data and returns a decision, and a thin shell that does the I/O. Write three tests for the pure part that use no mocks at all.

questions.prompt: Which function is **pure**?
options: `def add_fee(cents): return cents + 30`
`def greet(name): print(f"hi {name}")`
`def next_id(): global counter; counter += 1; return counter`
`def stamp(order): order.updated = time.time(); return order`
questions.explain: `add_fee` depends only on its argument and changes nothing outside itself. `greet` performs I/O, `stamp` mutates its input and reads the clock, and `next_id` reads and writes a global, so calling it twice gives different results.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
from functools import reduce

words = ["deep", "module", "api", "go"]
long_words = filter(lambda w: len(w) > 2, words)
print(reduce(lambda acc, w: acc + len(w), long_words, 0))
questions.explain: filter keeps `deep`, `module` and `api` (lengths 4, 6, 3) and drops `go`. reduce starts at 0 and adds each length: 0 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 13. Without the starting value 0, reduce would try to add a string to an int on the first step.

questions.prompt: This helper is not pure. What does this print?
questions.code:
def add_tag(tags, t):
    tags.append(t)
    return tags

base = ["py"]
a = add_tag(base, "go")
b = add_tag(base, "rs")
print(a)
questions.explain: `add_tag` mutates and returns the same list object, so `base`, `a` and `b` are all one list. The second call changes what `a` shows even though `a` was assigned earlier. A pure version, `return [*tags, t]`, would make `a` equal `['py', 'go']`.

questions.prompt: You need to test the rule "customers who have not ordered in 90 days get a win-back email". Which design is better and why?
options: A, because mocking the database and email client is the standard way to test
B, because the decision is a pure function of plain data and a date, so tests just call it with values; the shell is too thin to need much testing
A, because it keeps everything in one function
B, because it runs faster
questions.explain: B is functional core, imperative shell: the business rule can be tested with three lines per case and no mocks, and it cannot accidentally send email during a test. A forces every test to patch the clock, the database and the mailer. Speed is not the main benefit; testability and clarity are.

Values never change after creation; you build new ones.
Transform every element / keep some / combine into one value.

lessons.title: Rust: ownership and borrowing
lessons.objective: By the end you can predict whether a short Rust program compiles under the ownership and borrowing rules, and choose between taking ownership, borrowing and cloning in a function signature.
concept: Rust manages memory without a garbage collector, using three rules: each value has one **owner**; there is only one owner at a time; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (freed). Assigning a heap-owning value such as a `String` or `Vec` to another variable, or passing it to a function by value, **moves** ownership, and the old variable can no longer be used. The compiler rejects any later use with error E0382. Small `Copy` types such as `i32`, `bool` and `f64` are copied instead of moved.

To use a value without taking ownership you **borrow** it with a reference. The rules: at any moment you can have *either* any number of shared references `&T` *or* exactly one mutable reference `&mut T`, and a reference must never outlive the value it points to. The **borrow checker** enforces this at compile time, which rules out use-after-free, double frees and data races in safe code. Signatures announce intent: `fn len(s: &str)` reads, `fn push(v: &mut Vec<i32>)` modifies, `fn consume(s: String)` takes ownership.

Ownership is a design tool as well as a memory technique. A method that takes `self` by value, like a builder's `build(self)` or `BufWriter::into_inner(self)`, makes it impossible to use the old value afterwards, so misuse becomes a compile error. When the borrow checker objects, the usual fixes are: borrow instead of move (`&s`); clone deliberately when you truly need two owners (`s.clone()`); end a borrow before the next mutation by shortening its scope; or restructure so one place owns the data and others receive references.

rows: Move: t is the new owner
Deep copy: two owners of two strings
Not while m is in use

example.explain: The signatures tell the story: `word_count` only reads, so it borrows; `shout` consumes its input and hands back a new `String`. Uncommenting the last line fails to compile because `note` no longer owns anything.

lessons.tryit: Install Rust with rustup and write `fn longest_line(text: &str) -> &str`, which returns the longest line of its input. Then deliberately trigger three compiler errors: use a `String` after moving it, hold a `&mut` and a `&` to the same value at once, and return a reference to a local `String`. Copy each error code and write one sentence on which rule it enforces.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Rust's borrowing rule?
options: References are checked at run time and panic on conflicts
You can have one shared reference and one mutable reference at the same time
At any time you can have either any number of shared references (`&T`) or exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`), not both
You can have any number of mutable references as long as you do not read through them
questions.explain: Many readers or one writer, never both: that is what lets the compiler rule out data races and dangling pointers. The checks happen at compile time, not run time (`RefCell` moves them to run time, but plain references do not).

questions.prompt: Does this program compile?
options: No: `vec!` cannot be assigned to a variable
Yes, and it prints 3
No: `v` was moved into `w`, so `v.len()` is a use of a moved value (E0382)
Yes, because `w` and `v` share the same vector
questions.explain: `Vec` owns heap memory and is not `Copy`, so `let w = v;` moves ownership to `w` and makes `v` unusable. Rust never lets two variables own the same heap value. Writing `let w = v.clone();` or `let w = &v;` would make it compile.

questions.prompt: Does this program compile?
options: No: integers cannot be borrowed
Yes, but it panics at run time
Yes, it prints 10
No: `first` is a shared borrow of `scores` that is still used later, so `scores.push(30)` cannot take a mutable borrow (E0502)
questions.explain: `push` may reallocate the vector's buffer, which would leave `first` pointing at freed memory. Rust prevents this at compile time: a mutable borrow cannot coexist with a live shared borrow. Moving the `println!` above the `push`, or copying the value with `let first = scores[0];`, fixes it.

questions.prompt: A function only writes a message to a socket. Which signature is better and why?
options: `fn send(msg: &str)`, because it only needs to read; callers keep ownership and can pass a literal, a `&String` or a slice without cloning
`fn send(msg: &mut String)`, because sockets modify data
`fn send(msg: Box<String>)`, because heap data must be boxed
`fn send(msg: String)`, because owning the data is always faster
questions.explain: Borrowing as `&str` states that the function reads and does not keep the data, and accepts the widest range of inputs. Taking `String` forces callers who still need the message to clone it. `&mut` falsely announces mutation, and `Box<String>` adds a pointer for no reason.

lessons.why: Rust's ownership rules give memory safety without a garbage collector. Learning them changes how you think about who owns data in every language.

terms.d: The single variable responsible for a value; it's dropped when the owner leaves scope.
Assigning or passing a value transfers ownership; the old name can't be used.
A reference: many shared `&T` or exactly one mutable `&mut T`, never both.
The compiler check that enforces these rules.

mistakes.wrong: Cloning everything is the fix for borrow checker errors.
mistakes.right: Cloning works but hides design problems and costs memory. Prefer borrowing when you don't need ownership.

mistakes.wrong: I can hold a mutable reference while also reading through another reference.
mistakes.right: Shared and mutable references can't overlap; that rule is what prevents data races.

lessons.title: Go: goroutines and channels
lessons.objective: By the end you can write a bounded worker pool in Go with goroutines, channels and a WaitGroup, and predict when a channel program deadlocks.
concept: Go's concurrency is built on **goroutines**: functions started with the `go` keyword that the Go runtime schedules onto a small number of OS threads. Each starts with a stack of a few kilobytes that grows as needed, so a program can run hundreds of thousands of them. Goroutines communicate through **channels**, typed pipes where `ch <- v` sends and `v := <-ch` receives. A Go proverb sums up the approach: "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating."

An **unbuffered** channel, `make(chan int)`, makes the sender wait until a receiver takes the value, so every send is also a synchronization point. A **buffered** channel, `make(chan int, 10)`, lets up to 10 sends complete without a receiver. The sender should `close(ch)` when no more values will come, so receivers can loop with `for v := range ch`. If every goroutine is blocked, the runtime stops with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`. `sync.WaitGroup` waits for a group of goroutines, and `select` waits on several channels or a timeout.

The workhorse pattern is the **worker pool**: a jobs channel, N workers ranging over it, and a results channel. It bounds concurrency, so you never open 10,000 connections at once, and it is easy to reason about. State shared outside channels still needs a `sync.Mutex`, and `go test -race` or `go run -race` detects data races while the program runs. Always know how each goroutine will exit: one blocked forever on a channel nobody reads is a leak that slowly eats memory.

example.explain: Every goroutine has a clear exit: the producer after sending five jobs, each worker when `jobs` is closed, the closer after `wg.Wait()`, and `main` when `results` is closed. The order of results varies between runs, but the sum 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 55 does not.

lessons.tryit: Install Go and write a program that fetches 20 URLs using a pool of 4 workers, printing each status code and the total time. Run it with `go run -race .`. Then delete the `close(jobs)` line, run it again, and write down exactly what happens and why.

questions.prompt: What happens when a goroutine sends on an **unbuffered** channel?
options: The sender blocks until another goroutine receives the value
The program panics
The value is dropped if nobody is receiving
The value is stored and the sender continues immediately
questions.explain: An unbuffered channel has no storage, so a send completes only when a receiver takes the value; that hand-off is what makes it a synchronization point. Buffered channels store values up to their capacity. Go never silently drops a channel value.

questions.prompt: What happens when this program runs?
questions.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    ch := make(chan int)
    ch <- 1
    fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
options: It does not compile
It stops with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` because the send blocks forever: no other goroutine exists to receive
It prints 0
It prints 1
questions.explain: The send on the unbuffered channel waits for a receiver, but the only goroutine is `main`, which is stuck on that send and never reaches `<-ch`. The runtime detects that every goroutine is blocked and aborts. With `make(chan int, 1)` the send would complete into the buffer and the program would print 1.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
options: `ba`
`ab`
Nothing; it deadlocks
questions.explain: Both sends fit in the buffer of capacity 2, so neither blocks. Closing the channel does not discard buffered values: `range` receives `a` then `b` in order and stops when the closed channel is empty. Without `close`, the loop would block after `b` and the program would deadlock.

questions.prompt: You must resize 10,000 photos; each resize decodes a 50 MB image into memory and is CPU-bound. Which design is better and why?
options: One goroutine per photo, protected by a single mutex around the resize
Start one goroutine per photo, because goroutines are cheap
A worker pool with about `runtime.NumCPU()` workers reading from a jobs channel, because it bounds memory to a few images at a time and CPU-bound work cannot go faster than the number of cores
Process them one at a time in `main`, because concurrency is risky
questions.explain: Goroutines themselves are cheap, but the work inside them is not: 10,000 concurrent decodes could need hundreds of gigabytes of memory, and with CPU-bound work extra goroutines beyond the core count only add contention. Sequential processing wastes the other cores, and a mutex around the resize serializes the work while still holding every goroutine's memory.

video.title: Google I/O 2012 - Go Concurrency Patterns (Rob Pike)

lessons.why: Go's goroutines and channels make concurrent servers and pipelines straightforward. The worker-pool pattern bounds concurrency in any language.

terms.d: A lightweight function run concurrently with `go f()`.
A typed pipe between goroutines; unbuffered sends wait for a receiver.
Waits for a set of goroutines to finish.
N goroutines reading jobs from one channel, bounding concurrency.

mistakes.wrong: Goroutines are free, so start one per item.
mistakes.right: Unbounded goroutines can exhaust connections or memory. Bound them with a worker pool.

mistakes.wrong: Ranging over a channel ends when the sender stops sending.
mistakes.right: It ends only when the channel is closed. Forgetting `close` deadlocks the receiver.

takeaways: Unbuffered channels synchronise; buffered ones decouple.
Close the jobs channel when done sending, and wait for workers.
Every receive needs a sender, or the program deadlocks.

lessons.title: Error handling philosophies
lessons.objective: By the end you can compare exceptions, Go error values and Rust Result types, and design an API that separates expected failures from bugs and adds context as errors propagate.
concept: Languages disagree about how failure should travel. With **exceptions** (Python, Java, JavaScript), a failure unwinds the stack until some handler catches it. The happy path stays uncluttered, but a function's signature does not tell you what it can raise, so failures are easy to forget and can surface far from their cause. Python's guidance is to catch the narrowest exception you can actually handle, and never to write a bare `except:`, which also swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` and hides real bugs.

**Errors as values** make failure part of the return type. Go functions return `(value, error)` and callers check `if err != nil`, adding context as the error travels up with `fmt.Errorf("load config %s: %w", path, err)`; `errors.Is` and `errors.As` inspect the wrapped chain. Rust's `Result<T, E>` is an enum the compiler makes you handle, and the `?` operator propagates errors concisely, while `Option<T>` replaces null. The trade-off is more visible ceremony in exchange for every failure path being explicit and reviewable.

In any language the design questions are the same. Separate **expected failures** (file missing, invalid input, card declined), which belong in the interface for callers to handle, from **bugs** (broken invariants, impossible states), which should fail loudly with `panic!` or `assert` rather than be handled. Add context at each layer so the final message tells a story. And, as Ousterhout advises, **define errors out of existence** where you can: `dict.get(key, default)`, or a delete that succeeds when the item is already gone, removes an error case for every caller.

visual.title: Three ways to fail
rows: Manual if err != nil, wrap with %w

example.explain: Each layer adds what it knows (which file, which step) and wraps with `%w`, so the caller can still recognise the underlying `fs.ErrNotExist`. A missing file is an expected case with a sensible default; a malformed file is reported with a message that says exactly where it went wrong.

lessons.tryit: Write the same function three ways: Python with exceptions, Go with `(int, error)`, and Rust with `Result`. It reads a file of integers, one per line, and returns their sum, failing clearly on a missing file and on a non-numeric line, reporting the line number. Compare how much code each takes and how a caller finds out which failures are possible.

questions.prompt: In Go, what does the `%w` verb in `fmt.Errorf("read %s: %w", path, err)` do?
options: Formats the error in bold
Writes the error to a log file
Converts the error to a warning
Wraps `err` inside the new error, so `errors.Is` and `errors.As` can still find the original error in the chain
questions.explain: `%w` adds context while keeping the original error inspectable; with `%v` the message would be the same but the chain would be broken, so `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` would return false. It has nothing to do with formatting style or logging.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `"8080"` parses and is in range, so it returns the int 8080. `"http"` makes `int()` raise `ValueError`, which is caught inside `parse_port`, so it returns `None`. `"70000"` parses, but the range check raises a new `ValueError` outside the `try`, which propagates to the caller's handler, which stores its message.

questions.prompt: A background job sends a welcome email after signup. Which version is better and why?
questions.code:
# Version A
try:
    user = repo.get(user_id)
    send_welcome(user)
except Exception:
    pass

# Version B
user = repo.get(user_id)
if user is None:
    return  # deleted between signup and this job: expected, nothing to do
send_welcome(user)  # network errors propagate; the job runner retries them
options: A, because the job should never crash
B, because it handles the one expected case explicitly and lets real failures reach the job runner, which can retry and alert; A silently hides network errors, bugs and typos alike
B, because `None` checks are faster than exceptions
A, because B has more lines
questions.explain: `except Exception: pass` turns every failure, including an `AttributeError` from a typo, into a silent no-op, so welcome emails can stop for weeks with no signal. B states which failure is expected and why, and lets the rest propagate to code that can handle it. Line count and micro-speed are irrelevant.

questions.prompt: A cart API's `remove_item(cart_id, item_id)` currently raises `ItemNotInCart` when the item is absent. Callers are mobile clients that retry on timeouts, so they often remove the same item twice. Which change best applies "define errors out of existence"?
options: Make clients check whether the item is present before removing it
Document the exception more clearly
Make removal idempotent: removing an item that is not in the cart succeeds and leaves the cart unchanged, because the caller's goal (item not in cart) is already met
Return an error code instead of raising
questions.explain: The caller wants the item gone; if it already is, there is nothing to report. Idempotent removal removes the error case for every caller and makes retries safe. Documenting or changing the error's form keeps the case alive, and check-then-remove adds a race between the check and the removal.

resource.title: The Go Blog: Error handling and Go

video.title: Error handling in Rust: from first principles (Luca Palmieri)

lessons.why: How failure travels shapes every API you design. Separating expected failures from bugs and adding context makes errors actionable instead of mysterious.

terms.d: Failures unwind the stack until something catches them.
Failure is in the return type: Go's `(value, error)`, Rust's `Result<T, E>`.
Missing file or invalid input vs a broken invariant in your code.
Wrapping an error with what was being attempted as it travels up.

mistakes.wrong: Catching every exception makes code robust.
mistakes.right: It hides bugs. Handle expected failures; let bugs crash loudly with good context.

mistakes.wrong: Returning a bare 'failed' error is enough.
mistakes.right: Add context at each layer, like 'loading config from /etc/app.toml: permission denied'.

takeaways: Put expected failures in the interface; treat bugs differently.
Add context as errors move up.
Where possible, define errors out of existence with better APIs.

lessons.title: Type systems as design tools
lessons.objective: By the end you can replace combinations of flags and optional fields with a sum type, and use parse-don't-validate to push checks to the boundary of your program.
concept: Types are more than bug catchers: they are documentation that cannot go stale and a way to make invalid states impossible to build. The slogan is **make illegal states unrepresentable**. A fetch state stored as `loading: bool`, `data: dict | None` and `error: str | None` allows eight combinations, and most are nonsense: loading *and* failed? data *and* an error? Every function that touches it has to defend against the nonsense cases, and some function eventually forgets to.

**Algebraic data types** fix this. A *product type* (struct, tuple, dataclass) holds this AND that. A *sum type* (a Rust `enum`, a TypeScript discriminated union, a Python union of dataclasses) holds this OR that, and each variant carries only its own data. `enum Fetch { Loading, Loaded(Vec<Row>), Failed(String) }` has exactly three states, and `match` makes you handle all of them. Add a variant later and the compiler lists every place to update, turning an unknown unknown into a to-do list.

The companion idea is **parse, don't validate**, from Alexis King: instead of checking input and passing the same raw `str` onward, convert it once at the boundary into a type that proves the check happened, such as `EmailAddress`, `NonEmptyList` or `UserId`. Code further in takes the precise type and never re-checks. In Python, frozen dataclasses that validate in `__post_init__`, `typing.NewType`, `Literal`, and a checker like mypy or pyright (with `assert_never` for exhaustiveness) give you much of this; Rust and TypeScript enforce more of it at compile time.

left.title: Flags and optionals
points: loading: bool, data: dict | None, error: str | None
8 combinations, 3 meaningful
Every reader must guard against nonsense
New state means hunting for every if

right.title: Sum type
points: Loading | Loaded(rows) | Failed(message)
Exactly 3 states
Each variant carries only its own data
New variant: the checker lists every match to fix

example.explain: Each state carries only the data that makes sense for it: there is no `rows` field to forget to check when loading. With mypy or pyright, adding `case _: assert_never(state)` makes a forgotten variant a type error rather than a silent `None` return.

lessons.tryit: Find a type in your full-stack app with two or more booleans or optional fields that are only valid in certain combinations, such as an order's status, a fetch state or a subscription. Rewrite it as a sum type in TypeScript or Python, run your type checker, and fix every place it flags. Count how many impossible states you removed.

questions.prompt: What is a **sum type**?
options: A numeric type that supports addition
A type whose value is exactly one of several variants, each with its own data, like a Rust `enum` or a TypeScript discriminated union
A type that can be `null`
A type that holds several fields at once, like a struct
questions.explain: Sum types are "this OR that"; structs and tuples are product types, "this AND that". The name comes from counting values: a sum type has as many values as its variants' counts added together. Nullable types are a special case (a value or nothing), not the general idea.

questions.prompt: This type parses an email at the boundary. What does this print?
questions.explain: The raw string contains `@`, so validation passes, and `__post_init__` then stores the normalized form, stripped and lowercased. `object.__setattr__` is needed because the dataclass is frozen. Every `Email` that exists is therefore valid and normalized, so downstream code never has to check again.

questions.prompt: Which shipping API is better and why?
options: A, because B needs more types
B, because a `PaidOrder` can only be obtained from `charge()`, so "shipping an unpaid order" or "shipping without an address" cannot even be written; A relies on every caller passing honest flags
They are equivalent if A has good tests
A, because booleans are simpler than classes
questions.explain: B moves the rule into the type system: the check happens once, at `charge()`, and the type carries proof of it. In A, `ship(order_id, True, None)` type-checks and fails at run time, or worse, ships an unpaid order. Tests can catch some misuse in A, but B makes the misuse impossible to express.

questions.prompt: A `User` has `is_admin: bool` and `is_guest: bool`, and a guest can never be an admin. How many combinations can the two fields represent, and how many are valid?
options: 4 combinations, 4 valid
4 combinations, 3 valid; an `enum Role { Guest, Member, Admin }` represents exactly the 3
3 combinations, 2 valid
2 combinations, 2 valid
questions.explain: Two booleans give 2 x 2 = 4 combinations: (false, false) member, (true, false) admin, (false, true) guest, and (true, true), the impossible guest-admin. A three-variant enum makes the fourth state unrepresentable, so no code needs to check for it.

video.title: Parse, Don't Validate

lessons.why: Types that make illegal states unrepresentable remove whole categories of bugs and checks. Parsing at the boundary means the rest of your code can trust its data.

terms.d: Holds this AND that: a struct, tuple or dataclass.
Is this OR that: a Rust enum or a TypeScript discriminated union.
Design types so invalid combinations can't be built.
Convert raw input once into a type that proves it's valid.

mistakes.wrong: A few boolean flags and optional fields are flexible.
mistakes.right: They allow impossible combinations like `loading` and `error` both true. Use a sum type.

mistakes.wrong: Validating input in each function is safest.
mistakes.right: Parse once at the boundary into a precise type, then pass that type around.

takeaways: Replace flag combinations with a sum type.
Parse at the edges; trust the types inside.
Types are documentation that can't go stale.

project.title: A grep clone in Rust or Go
project.brief: Build `seek`, a command-line search tool in the spirit of grep, in Rust or Go. It exercises the module's ideas in a new language: typed configuration, errors as values, ownership or goroutines, and a pure matching core with an I/O shell.
milestones: `seek PATTERN FILE...` prints matching lines prefixed with `file:`, and exits with 0 if anything matched, 1 if nothing matched, and 2 on error, like grep.
Add `-i` (ignore case), `-n` (line numbers), `-v` (invert) and `-r` (recurse into directories), parsing arguments into a typed `Config` struct with `clap` (Rust) or `flag` (Go).
Handle errors as values: an unreadable file prints `seek: <path>: <reason>` to stderr and the search continues; no `unwrap()` or ignored `err` on anything user-controlled.
Keep the matching logic pure (a function from a line and a config to a bool) with unit tests, and add integration tests that run the binary on a fixture directory.
Search files in parallel (a worker pool in Go, threads or `rayon` in Rust) so that output lines from different files never interleave mid-line.
Benchmark against `grep -r` on a large tree such as a CPython checkout using `hyperfine`, and write a README with usage examples and a note on one ownership or concurrency decision.
project.stretch: Add regular expressions and a `--json` output mode, and get within 2x of ripgrep's time on your benchmark.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
nums = [5, 2, 8, 1]
print(list(map(lambda n: n * 2, filter(lambda n: n > 2, nums))))
exam.explain: filter runs first and keeps 5 and 8, the only values greater than 2; map then doubles them to 10 and 16. Reading the expression inside-out (filter, then map) is the usual way to follow nested map and filter calls.

exam.prompt: Does this Rust program compile?
options: No: the first `print_len(name)` moves `name` into the function, so the second call uses a moved value; changing the parameter to `&str` and calling `print_len(&name)` fixes it
No: `String::from` is not allowed in `main`
Yes, it prints 6 twice
Yes, because `print_len` does not modify the string
exam.explain: Passing a `String` by value moves it, whether or not the callee modifies it. After the first call, `name` owns nothing. Borrowing with `&str` expresses what the function actually needs, a read-only view, and lets the caller keep ownership.

exam.prompt: What happens when this Go program runs?
options: It does not compile because the buffer is too small
It deadlocks before printing anything
It prints `123` and exits normally
It prints `123`, then stops with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` because the channel is never closed, so `range` keeps waiting
exam.explain: The three sends fit in the buffer, so they complete. `range` receives 1, 2 and 3, then waits for a fourth value or a close. No other goroutine exists to provide either, so the runtime reports a deadlock. Adding `close(ch)` before the loop makes it exit normally.

exam.prompt: In Rust, what does the `?` operator do when applied to a `Result`?
options: It converts the `Result` into an `Option`
It panics if the result is an error
If the value is `Ok(v)` it evaluates to `v`; if it is `Err(e)` it returns early from the current function with that error (converted with `From` if needed)
It ignores the error and continues
exam.explain: `?` is concise error propagation: it unwraps success and returns failure to the caller, so the enclosing function must itself return a compatible `Result`. Panicking is what `unwrap()` does; ignoring errors is not something `?` ever does.

exam.prompt: Which Go snippet handles the error better and why?
options: B, because `%w` makes the program faster
A, because `os.ReadFile` never fails in production
A, because it is shorter
B, because A discards the error, so a missing or unreadable file silently becomes an empty config; B adds context and lets the caller decide
exam.explain: Assigning the error to `_` throws away the only signal that something went wrong, and `data` will be empty, producing a confusing failure much later. B fails at the point of the problem with a message naming the file, and `%w` keeps the original error inspectable with `errors.Is`. Speed has nothing to do with it.

exam.prompt: Module 2 taught you to introduce seams before writing characterization tests. How does the functional core, imperative shell style change that?
options: It makes tests unnecessary
It requires mocking more dependencies
Core logic is already a pure function of plain data, so it needs no seams or mocks: tests call it directly with values; only the thin shell touches the clock, database and network
It only works in Haskell
exam.explain: A seam exists to substitute dependencies such as clocks and databases. Pure functions receive everything as arguments, so they are seams by construction. Tests are still necessary, just much simpler. The style works in any language, including Python, Go and Rust.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: `replace` builds a new `Point` with `x=2` and leaves `p` untouched. Assigning to a field of a frozen dataclass raises `FrozenInstanceError`, so `p.x` stays 1. Immutability means changes produce new values, never edits to existing ones.

exam.prompt: A payment record has `status: str`, `failure_reason: str | None` and `refunded_at: datetime | None`. Bugs keep appearing where a failed payment has a refund date. Which change best prevents this class of bug?
options: Rename `refunded_at` to `refunded_at_if_refunded`
Add an `is_valid()` method and hope callers use it
Add a comment explaining which combinations are valid
Model it as a sum type: `Pending | Succeeded(paid_at) | Failed(reason) | Refunded(paid_at, refunded_at)`, so a failed payment has no refund field at all
exam.explain: The bug is an illegal state that the current type allows. A sum type removes it entirely, and a type checker then forces every `match` to consider each real state. Comments, opt-in validators and renames all leave the illegal state representable.

modules.title: Debugging & performance
modules.summary: Find bugs and slowdowns by experiment instead of guesswork: scientific debugging, bisect, profilers, honest benchmarks and production observability.

lessons.title: The scientific debugging method
lessons.objective: By the end you can debug by writing explicit hypotheses, predictions and experiments in a log, starting from a shrunk reproduction, instead of changing code until the symptom disappears.
concept: Debugging by guessing, changing things until the symptom goes away, is slow and often leaves the real bug in place. The scientific method is faster. **Observe** the failure precisely. Form a **hypothesis** about the cause. Derive a **prediction** the hypothesis implies ("if the cache key ignores the locale, a French user loading the page right after an English user will see English text"). Run an **experiment** that tests it, and conclude: the hypothesis is refuted or it survives. Write every step in a debugging log so you never retest an idea you already ruled out.

Everything starts with a reliable **reproduction**. Then shrink it: remove inputs, steps and code until you have the smallest case that still fails; the cause often becomes obvious on the way. If it only happens in production, list what differs: data, configuration, versions, concurrency, time zones. Then **narrow the search space** by halves: bisect the input, disable half the code path, or bisect history with `git bisect` (next lesson). A good experiment rules out about half of the remaining possibilities, whichever way it turns out.

Check your assumptions explicitly, because the bug lives in the one you did not check. Is the code you are reading the code that is running, or is it a stale build, a different virtualenv or a cached container image? Is the configuration what you think? Print it. Read the whole error message and stack trace. Explaining the problem line by line to someone else, or to a rubber duck, forces you to state assumptions out loud. When you find the cause, write a failing test before the fix, so the bug can never quietly return.

steps.label: Predict
steps.detail: If true, then X must happen

steps.label: Experiment
steps.detail: Test the prediction; log the result

steps.label: Fix with a test
steps.detail: Failing test first, then the fix

example.code:
BUG-212  Some invoices show total $0.00
Repro:  invoice 8841 in staging, every time. Shrunk to one line item, qty=3, price=0.33

H1: rounding happens per item before multiplying
    Predict: 0.33 x 3 = 0.99, not 0.00.  Experiment: compute by hand.  Refuted.
H2: qty arrives as the string "3" and the template swallows the TypeError
    Predict: type(qty) is str at render time.
    Experiment: log type(qty) in the template context -> <class 'str'>.  Survives.
Fix: coerce qty in InvoiceLine.__post_init__; added test_qty_from_csv_is_int first.
example.explain: Each hypothesis has a prediction that could fail, and the log records which ones did. The first experiment took one minute and ruled out a whole area. The fix came with a test that failed before it.

lessons.tryit: Take the last bug you fixed, or one from your issue tracker, and rewrite its story as a debugging log in the format of the example: reproduction, each hypothesis with its prediction, the experiment and the result. For your next real bug, keep the log as you go and count how many experiments it took.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the scientific debugging loop?
options: Fix, test, hypothesize, observe
Hypothesize, fix, deploy, observe
Observe and reproduce, hypothesize, predict, experiment, conclude
Experiment, observe, predict, hypothesize
questions.explain: You need a precise observation and a reproduction before a hypothesis is meaningful, and a prediction before the experiment so that the result can refute something. Fixing before understanding is the guess-and-check approach this method replaces.

questions.prompt: Users report that a new cart sometimes already contains items they never added. Predict the output.
questions.code:
def add_item(item, cart=[]):
    cart.append(item)
    return cart

add_item("pen")
print(add_item("pad"))
questions.explain: A default argument is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call that omits `cart` shares the same list. The second call appends to the list that already holds `pen`. The fix is `cart=None` with `cart = [] if cart is None else cart` inside the function, plus a test that two default calls return independent carts.

questions.prompt: An export fails only in production, for about 1 in 50 users. You suspect the user's data, the time zone setting, or a library version difference. Which first experiment is best?
options: Upgrade every library to the latest version and redeploy
Run the export locally against a copy of one failing user's data with the production library versions and time zone; whichever way it turns out, it splits the hypotheses
Rewrite the export code to be more robust
Add try/except around the export and log "failed"
questions.explain: Reproducing one failing case under production-like conditions tests all three hypotheses at once: if it fails locally, you can vary data, time zone and versions one at a time; if it does not, the difference lies in the environment. Rewriting and upgrading change many things blindly, and a generic log line adds no information about the cause.

questions.prompt: Your fix passes locally, but after deploying, the bug still happens in staging exactly as before. What should you check first?
options: Whether the tests are wrong
Whether staging is running your new code at all, for example a version endpoint, the image tag, or a log line added by the fix
Whether you should revert and try a different fix
Whether the bug is actually in a different function
questions.explain: Unchanged behaviour after a fix is the classic sign of a broken assumption about what is running: a stale image, a cached build or a deploy to the wrong environment. That is cheap to check and invalidates every other conclusion if it is wrong. Only once you know the new code is running is it worth doubting the fix.
