video.title: Debugging: Scientific Method

lessons.why: Guess-and-check debugging is slow and often leaves the real bug in place. A written hypothesis log finds causes faster and makes hard bugs tractable.

terms.d: A reliable way to make the bug happen, shrunk to the smallest case.
A specific, testable explanation of the cause.
What you'll see if the hypothesis is true.
The cheapest observation that confirms or rejects it.

mistakes.wrong: If I change things until it works, the bug is fixed.
mistakes.right: You may have hidden the symptom. Explain the cause and confirm it with a prediction.

mistakes.wrong: The code I'm reading is the code that's running.
mistakes.right: Check for stale builds, cached files, the wrong branch or a different config.

takeaways: Reproduce, shrink, hypothesise, predict, experiment, conclude.
Write each step in a debugging log.
Check your assumptions explicitly; the bug lives in the one you skipped.

lessons.title: Finding the breaking commit with git bisect
lessons.objective: By the end you can use `git bisect`, manually and with `git bisect run`, to find the commit that introduced a regression, and avoid the traps that make it point at the wrong commit.
concept: When something worked last month and is broken now, the cause was introduced by one of the commits in between, and `git bisect` finds it by binary search. You mark one known-good and one known-bad commit; git checks out the midpoint; you test it and mark it good or bad; git halves the range again. With 1,000 commits in the range you need about 10 tests, since 2 to the power 10 is 1,024. The answer is the exact commit that introduced the change, usually small enough to make the cause obvious.

The manual loop: `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad` (the current checkout is broken), `git bisect good v2.3.0` (that release worked), then test each checkout and answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`. Use `git bisect skip` for a commit that cannot be tested, for example one that does not build, and `git bisect reset` to return to where you started. Bisect is only as good as your test: it must reliably tell good from bad, so build a shrunk reproduction first.

Automate with `git bisect run <cmd>`: git runs the command at each step and treats exit code 0 as good, 125 as skip, and any other code from 1 to 127 as bad. A script that runs a single test turns an afternoon of checking into a few unattended minutes. Keep that script outside the repository, because each checkout changes the tracked files. This only works if your history consists of small commits that each build and pass tests, the discipline from module 3. Custom terms (`--term-old`, `--term-new`) let you hunt for when something got faster or changed, not just when it broke.

steps.label: Culprit
steps.detail: First bad commit, then git bisect reset

example.code:
cp tests/test_export.py /tmp/check_unicode.py   # keep the test outside the repo
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD               # broken now
git bisect good v2.3.0            # worked in this release
git bisect run pytest -x -q /tmp/check_unicode.py
# git prints: "<sha> is the first bad commit", with its message and changed files
git show <sha>                    # read the culprit
git bisect reset                  # back to where you started
example.explain: Copying the test out of the repository means every checkout runs the same check, even commits from before the test existed. `git bisect run` does the rest unattended and prints the first bad commit.

lessons.tryit: Make a practice repository: write a short script that creates 64 commits, each appending a line to `calc.py`, with one commit in the middle introducing an off-by-one error. Write a test for it, then find the culprit twice, once manually and once with `git bisect run`, and record how many steps each took.

questions.prompt: During `git bisect run`, what does an exit code of 125 from your script mean?
options: Abort the bisect
The commit is good
The commit is bad
This commit cannot be tested, so skip it
questions.explain: 125 is reserved for skip, typically used when the commit does not build. 0 means good, and any other code from 1 to 127 means bad. Codes above 127 abort the bisect, which is why scripts that crash in unusual ways can stop it.

questions.prompt: About how many test runs will `git bisect` need to search 300 commits between a good and a bad commit?
options: About 9
About 30
About 300
About 150
questions.explain: Each test halves the range, so it takes the smallest n with 2 to the power n at least 300, which is 9 (2 to the 9 is 512). 150 is the average for a linear search, and 300 is its worst case, which is exactly what bisect avoids.

questions.prompt: You run `git bisect run pytest -q tests/test_export.py::test_unicode`. The test file was added only last week, but the good commit is from three months ago. What goes wrong?
options: In older commits the test file does not exist, so pytest exits with a usage error code (4), which bisect counts as bad, and bisect reports a wrong first bad commit. Copy the test to a script outside the repository and run that instead
Bisect automatically skips commits without the file
pytest exits with 0 when no file is found, so every old commit is marked good
Nothing; pytest finds the test in every commit
questions.explain: Bisect only sees exit codes: anything from 1 to 127 except 125 means bad, and pytest returns 4 when the given file or directory does not exist. So every old commit looks broken, and the "culprit" is meaningless. A test script stored outside the working tree is present at every checkout and tests the same thing each time.

questions.prompt: Halfway through a manual bisect, the checked-out commit fails to compile because of an unrelated syntax error that was fixed in the next commit. What should you do?
options: `git bisect reset` and start again
`git bisect skip`
`git bisect bad`
`git bisect good`
questions.explain: You cannot tell whether this commit has the bug, so marking it either way would feed bisect false information and could send it to the wrong half. `skip` tells bisect to try a nearby commit instead. Resetting throws away the progress you already have.

video.title: Git bisect tutorial: how to find a bad commit

lessons.why: When something used to work, the breaking commit is the fastest route to the cause. Bisect finds it in log₂ of the number of commits.

terms.d: Binary search through history for the first bad commit.
Marks a commit as working or broken.
Automates the search with a script: exit 0 good, 125 skip, 1–127 bad.
Marks a commit that can't be tested, such as one that doesn't build.

mistakes.wrong: Bisect works with any history.
mistakes.right: It needs commits that build and a test that gives a consistent answer. Flaky tests point at the wrong commit.

mistakes.wrong: Any non-zero exit code means bad in `bisect run`.
mistakes.right: 125 means skip, and codes above 127 abort the bisect. Return 1 for bad.

takeaways: Mark one known good and one known bad commit, then test each checkout.
Automate with a script that exits 0, 1 or 125.
Atomic commits make bisect results meaningful.

lessons.title: Profiling and flame graphs
lessons.objective: By the end you can profile a slow Python program with cProfile and a sampling profiler, read a flame graph, and identify which function to optimize first.
concept: The first rule of performance work is **measure, don't guess**. Programmers are notoriously bad at predicting where time goes: the slow part is usually a hidden O(n squared) loop, repeated I/O or an innocent-looking library call, not the code that looks complicated. A **profiler** tells you where time is actually spent. Before touching anything, write down a baseline ("the export of 50,000 rows takes 41 s") and a target, so you know when you are done and can prove what each change bought.

There are two kinds. **Deterministic** profilers like Python's `cProfile` record every function call: `python -m cProfile -s cumulative app.py` prints call counts, `tottime` (time in the function itself) and `cumtime` (time including everything it calls). Counts are exact, but the instrumentation adds overhead. **Sampling** profilers like `py-spy`, Linux `perf` and Go's `pprof` interrupt the program many times per second and record the stack. Their overhead is low, so you can even attach to a running production process: `py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid 1234`.

A **flame graph**, popularized by Brendan Gregg, draws sampled stacks: each box is a function, the vertical axis is stack depth with callers below and callees above, and a box's **width** is the share of samples in which that function was on the stack. The horizontal axis is *not* time: boxes are sorted alphabetically so identical stacks merge. Look for wide boxes with nothing above them: a function burning CPU itself. A wide box low down whose width is split among many narrow children means the cost is spread out, so look higher.

visual.title: Profilers you will use
rows: Exact call counts in a local run
Live processes, flame graphs, low overhead

example.code:
import cProfile, pstats

def slow_unique(items):
    seen = []
    for x in items:
        if x not in seen:          # O(n) scan of a list for every item
            seen.append(x)
    return seen

def fast_unique(items):
    return list(dict.fromkeys(items))   # O(1) average lookups, keeps order

data = [i % 5000 for i in range(50_000)]
cProfile.run("slow_unique(data)", "prof.out")
pstats.Stats("prof.out").sort_stats("tottime").print_stats(5)
example.explain: Almost all the time shows up as `tottime` of `slow_unique` itself, because `x not in seen` is an operator, not a Python function call, so the profiler cannot show it separately. In a flame graph this appears as a wide box with nothing above it: the function is doing the work itself.

lessons.tryit: Profile one slow path in your own app, such as a page load, an export or a test that takes over a second, with `cProfile` and with `py-spy record` (or Chrome DevTools for front-end code). Save the flame graph, mark the widest top-of-stack frames, and write two sentences predicting what fixing each would save before you change any code.

questions.prompt: In a flame graph, what does the **width** of a box represent?
options: The number of lines of code in the function
The function's memory usage
The order in which functions ran
The proportion of samples in which that function was on the stack, so roughly its share of total time including callees
questions.explain: Width is the share of samples, so wide means expensive. The horizontal axis is not a timeline; frames are sorted alphabetically to merge identical stacks, which is a common misreading. Lines of code and memory are not encoded in a CPU flame graph.

questions.prompt: Based on this `cProfile` output, which function should you optimize first?
questions.code:
ncalls  tottime  cumtime  function
     1    0.002   12.410  export_csv
 50000    0.310   12.380  format_row
 50000   11.900   11.900  lookup_region
 50000    0.150    0.150  escape
options: `lookup_region`, because its own time (tottime) is 11.9 of the 12.4 seconds
`export_csv`, because it has the highest cumtime
`escape`, because it is called 50,000 times
`format_row`, because it is in the middle of the call chain
questions.explain: `cumtime` includes callees, so `export_csv` and `format_row` look expensive only because they call `lookup_region`. Its `tottime` of 11.9 s is where the time is actually spent. `escape` is called just as often but costs 0.15 s in total, so call count alone is misleading.

questions.prompt: A production API worker has become slow, and you cannot restart it without losing the state that triggers the problem. Which tool fits best?
options: Run the unit tests with `--durations`
Restart it under `python -m cProfile` and wait for the problem to recur
Add `print(time.time())` statements and redeploy
Attach a sampling profiler such as `py-spy record --pid <pid>` (or `py-spy dump` for a snapshot of current stacks), which needs no restart and adds little overhead
questions.explain: A sampling profiler can attach to a live process and observe the problem as it happens, with low overhead. cProfile requires starting the program under it and adds significant overhead. Prints and redeploys both lose the state you need, and unit-test durations tell you nothing about production behaviour.

questions.prompt: The profile showed a list-based dedupe as the hotspot, and it was replaced with this. What does it print?
questions.code: print(list(dict.fromkeys([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])))
questions.explain: `dict.fromkeys` keeps the first occurrence of each key, and dicts preserve insertion order, so the result is the unique values in first-seen order. Each membership check is O(1) on average instead of an O(n) scan of a list. `list(set(...))` would be fast too but does not guarantee order.

video.title: USENIX ATC '17: Visualizing Performance with Flame Graphs (Brendan Gregg)

lessons.why: Programmers are bad at guessing where time goes. A profiler tells you the one function worth optimising, so you don't waste days on the wrong one.

terms.d: Records every call, like `cProfile`; accurate counts, more overhead.
Samples stacks periodically, like py-spy; low overhead, works in production.
Sampled stacks drawn as boxes; width is time spent.
Time in a function including everything it calls.

mistakes.wrong: The tallest stack in a flame graph is the slowest part.
mistakes.right: Width shows time, not height. Look for wide boxes.

mistakes.wrong: I know which part is slow; profiling is overkill.
mistakes.right: The slow part is usually a surprise, like a hidden O(n²) or repeated I/O. Measure first.

takeaways: Measure, don't guess.
Sort `cProfile` by cumulative time to find expensive call trees.
In flame graphs, wide plateaus are where to look.

lessons.title: Benchmarking without fooling yourself
lessons.objective: By the end you can design a benchmark that controls for noise, warm-up and unrealistic data, report it as a distribution, and use Amdahl's law to predict the end-to-end effect of a speedup.
concept: A benchmark is an experiment, and most benchmarks are bad experiments. Common pitfalls: measuring only once, when noise from other processes, CPU frequency scaling and thermal throttling easily reaches 10 percent; including warm-up costs such as imports, JIT compilation or cold caches in the timing; using toy data, 10 rows when production has 10 million, so the complexity class never shows; and measuring the wrong thing, such as a cache that only ever sees one key, or a result the compiler optimizes away because nothing uses it.

Use tools that handle repetition and statistics for you. In Python, `timeit.repeat` runs a snippet many times, and `python -m timeit -s "setup" "stmt"` reports the best of several runs; `pyperf` adds calibration and outlier detection. For whole commands, `hyperfine 'old' 'new'` runs warm-ups and reports mean and standard deviation. Go has `go test -bench=. -benchmem`, and Rust has the `criterion` crate. Report distributions such as median and p95, compare on the same machine with the same data and build flags, and never benchmark a Rust debug build.

Microbenchmarks answer narrow questions, but users experience end-to-end latency. **Amdahl's law**: the overall speedup is limited by the fraction of time you did not improve. Making a function 10 times faster when it accounts for 2 percent of a request saves less than 2 percent. So profile first to find what matters, microbenchmark candidate fixes, then confirm with an end-to-end measurement on realistic data. Check that the faster version gives the same answer, and commit the benchmark script so anyone can rerun it after future changes.

visual.title: Benchmarking pitfalls
rows: Fast in the benchmark, slow in production

example.code:
import timeit

setup = "data = [i % 5000 for i in range(50_000)]"
for stmt in ["list(dict.fromkeys(data))", "list(set(data))", "sorted(set(data))"]:
    times = timeit.repeat(stmt, setup=setup, number=20, repeat=5)
    print(f"{stmt:28} best {min(times) / 20 * 1e3:.2f} ms")
example.explain: `repeat` gives five independent measurements of 20 runs each, and the minimum is the least disturbed by noise. Note that the three statements do not all compute the same thing: `list(set(data))` does not guarantee order, so even if it wins, it is only a valid replacement where order does not matter.

lessons.tryit: Benchmark two implementations of something in your own code, such as a lookup, a serializer or a query, in three ways: a single `time.time()` measurement, `timeit.repeat`, and `hyperfine` on a small script. Record all three results, explain any disagreement, and say which number you would put in a PR description and why.

questions.prompt: What does Amdahl's law say?
options: Memory access is slower than computation
Performance doubles every two years
The overall speedup from optimizing part of a program is limited by the fraction of time spent in the parts you did not optimize
A benchmark must be run at least 30 times
questions.explain: If 75 percent of the time is untouched, even an infinitely fast fix for the other 25 percent gives at most a 1.33x overall speedup. The doubling claim is a loose paraphrase of Moore's law, and the run count is a rule of thumb, not Amdahl's law.

questions.prompt: A request takes 200 ms, 25% of it in a function you made 10x faster. What does this print?
questions.code:
total_ms = 200
fraction = 0.25        # share of time in the optimized function
speedup = 10
new_ms = total_ms * (1 - fraction) + total_ms * fraction / speedup
print(round(new_ms, 1))
questions.explain: The untouched 75 percent still costs 150 ms, and the optimized 50 ms becomes 5 ms, so the request now takes 155 ms: about 1.29x faster, not 10x. This is Amdahl's law with real numbers, and why you profile end to end before celebrating a microbenchmark.

questions.prompt: A PR claims a new cache makes `get_user` 50x faster. The benchmark calls `get_user(42)` 1,000 times in a loop and compares against the uncached version. What is the main flaw?
options: It should use `time.time()` instead of `timeit`
1,000 iterations is too many

It measures only cache hits for one hot key: after the first call every lookup is a hit, while real traffic has many users, cold entries, evictions and invalidations, so the real speedup could be far smaller
Caches never make code faster
questions.explain: The benchmark's workload does not resemble production: one key gives a 99.9 percent hit rate. A fair benchmark replays a realistic key distribution and includes the cost of misses and invalidation. The iteration count is fine, `time.time()` is a worse timer, and caches certainly can help, which is why measuring them honestly matters.

questions.prompt: Five runs each: version A has mean 120 ms with standard deviation 40 ms; version B has mean 110 ms with standard deviation 45 ms. What can you conclude?
options: B is about 8% faster; ship it
Both are equally fast
A is faster because its standard deviation is lower
Nothing reliable yet: the difference is much smaller than the run-to-run spread, so you need more runs, a quieter machine, or a statistical comparison before claiming B is faster
questions.explain: A 10 ms difference with 40 to 45 ms of noise across only five runs is well within chance. Reducing noise (fixed CPU frequency, no other load) and taking more samples, then comparing distributions or using a test such as Mann-Whitney, are the honest next steps. Lower variance does not mean faster, and "equally fast" is also a claim the data cannot support.

lessons.why: A misleading benchmark can justify the wrong change. Controlling noise and thinking end to end keeps performance work honest.

terms.d: Initial runs affected by caches and JIT; exclude them.
Report median and spread across many runs, not one number.
Inputs matching production sizes and shapes.
Overall speedup is limited by the part you didn't improve.

mistakes.wrong: Running a benchmark once gives the answer.
mistakes.right: Noise from other processes and CPU scaling varies a lot. Repeat and report a distribution.

mistakes.wrong: Making a function 10× faster makes the program 10× faster.
mistakes.right: If it's 20% of runtime, the best overall speedup is about 1.25×.

takeaways: Repeat runs, discard warm-up, report median and spread.
Benchmark on realistic data.
Use Amdahl's law to decide whether an optimisation is worth it.

lessons.title: Observability in your own apps
lessons.objective: By the end you can add structured logs with request IDs and RED metrics to a web app, and use them to answer a question about a specific failed request.
concept: In production you cannot attach a debugger or add a print and rerun; you can only ask questions of the data your system already emits. **Observability** is how well you can answer new questions about the system's behaviour from those outputs. There are three main signals: **logs**, discrete events with context; **metrics**, numeric time series that are cheap to store and alert on, such as request counts and latency percentiles; and **traces**, the path of a single request through functions and services, recorded as a tree of timed **spans**.

Make logs **structured**: emit JSON key-value pairs such as `{"event": "payment_failed", "order_id": 8841, "provider": "stripe", "latency_ms": 2140}` rather than prose, so you can filter and aggregate them. Attach a **request ID** (or trace ID) to every log line produced while handling a request, and return it in a response header so a user's bug report can be tied to the exact log lines. Log at boundaries and decisions, not inside tight loops, and never log secrets, tokens, passwords or full card numbers.

For metrics, start with the **RED** method for every service: **Rate** (requests per second), **Errors** (failed requests per second) and **Duration** (the latency distribution, especially p50, p95 and p99, because averages hide the slow tail). **OpenTelemetry** is the vendor-neutral standard for emitting all three signals, with SDKs for Python, Go, Rust and JavaScript and automatic instrumentation for common frameworks. Alert on symptoms users feel, like error rate and p99 latency, not every CPU spike, and build the dashboard before the outage, not during it.

items.label: Logs
items.detail: Structured events: what happened, with context

items.label: Metrics
items.detail: RED: rate, errors, duration percentiles; cheap to alert on

items.label: Traces
items.detail: One request as a tree of timed spans across services

items.label: Request ID
items.detail: The thread tying a user's report to all three

example.code:
import json, logging, time, uuid

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("app")

def log_event(event, **fields):
    log.info(json.dumps({"event": event, "ts": round(time.time(), 3), **fields}))

def handle_checkout(order_id):
    request_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]     # also returned to the client as X-Request-ID
    start = time.perf_counter()
    status = "error"
    try:
        ...                                # charge card, write order
        status = "ok"
    except Exception as exc:
        log_event("checkout_failed", request_id=request_id, order_id=order_id,
                  error=type(exc).__name__)
        raise
    finally:
        log_event("checkout_done", request_id=request_id, order_id=order_id, status=status,
                  duration_ms=round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000, 1))
example.explain: Every line for the request carries the same `request_id`, so one search finds the full story. The `finally` block records status and duration whether the request succeeded or failed, which is exactly the data RED metrics are built from. The exception is logged with its type and then re-raised, not swallowed.

lessons.tryit: Add structured JSON logging with a per-request ID to one endpoint of your full-stack app, return the ID in an `X-Request-ID` response header, and record RED metrics for that endpoint (counters and a latency histogram exposed at `/metrics` are enough). Trigger an error on purpose, then find every log line for that request using only the ID.

questions.prompt: In the RED method, what do the letters stand for?
options: Requests, Exceptions, Disk
Reliability, Efficiency, Durability
Rate, Errors, Duration
Read, Execute, Deploy
questions.explain: RED is Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests per second) and Duration (the latency distribution). Together they describe what users of a request-driven service experience. The other expansions are invented.

questions.prompt: Ten request latencies in ms, one of them very slow. What does this print?
questions.code:
import statistics

latencies = [20, 22, 21, 19, 23, 20, 22, 21, 20, 900]
print(round(statistics.mean(latencies)), statistics.median(latencies))
questions.explain: The sum is 1,088, so the mean is 108.8, rounded to 109, which describes no real request: nine users waited about 20 ms and one waited 900 ms. The median is the average of the two middle values, 21 and 21, returned as the float 21.0. Percentiles like p50 and p99 show both facts at once; the mean blurs them.

questions.prompt: Which log line will be most useful when a user reports "checkout failed around 3pm" and gives you the request ID from the error page?
options: `Checkout failed for user ana@example.com with card 4242 4242 4242 4242`
`print("here 2")`
`ERROR something went wrong in checkout`
`{"event": "checkout_failed", "request_id": "7f3a9c2e1b40", "user_id": 512, "order_id": 8841, "error": "CardDeclined", "duration_ms": 2140}`
questions.explain: The structured line can be found by request ID, filtered by event or error type, and aggregated, and it carries the context needed to act. The vague line cannot be tied to the user's request. Logging an email address and a full card number is a privacy and compliance failure, and debug prints carry no context at all.

questions.prompt: Which alerting setup is better for a small web app and why?
options: Page when the error rate exceeds 2% or p99 latency exceeds 1 s for 5 minutes, and show CPU on a dashboard for diagnosis
No alerts; check the dashboard every morning
Page on every logged exception
Page the on-call developer whenever CPU exceeds 80% for one minute
questions.explain: Alerts should fire on symptoms users feel, held long enough to filter blips, so every page means real harm. High CPU may be completely harmless, such as a batch job, and paging on every exception creates noise people learn to ignore. No alerts means users find outages before you do.

terms.d: JSON key-value events instead of prose lines.
An id attached to every log line for one request, so you can follow it.
Rate, Errors and Duration for every service.
The path of one request through services, timed step by step.

mistakes.wrong: More log lines means better observability.
mistakes.right: Unstructured noise is hard to query. Log fewer, structured events with ids.

mistakes.wrong: Average latency tells me how the service performs.
mistakes.right: Averages hide slow requests. Track percentiles like p95 and p99.

takeaways: Attach a request ID to every log line.
Track Rate, Errors and Duration percentiles per service.
OpenTelemetry standardises traces, metrics and logs.

project.title: Make a slow program 10x faster
project.brief: Take a slow program, one of your own or a deliberately naive one such as a log analyzer that scans a list for every line, and make it at least 10 times faster end to end on realistic data. You will measure honestly, profile, change one thing at a time, and write a report that someone else could reproduce.
milestones: Build a realistic input (for example a 1 GB log file or a one-million-row CSV) and a benchmark script using hyperfine or `timeit`; record the baseline as mean and standard deviation.
Write a correctness check, such as a diff against a golden output file, that every optimized version must pass before it is timed.
Profile with cProfile and py-spy (or pprof); save flame graphs and list the top three hotspots with their share of total time.
Apply one optimization at a time, algorithms and data structures first, then I/O, then micro-optimizations, re-benchmarking after each and keeping a table of version, time and speedup.
Reach at least 10x end to end, or use Amdahl's law and your profiles to show why the remaining time cannot go lower.
Write a report of about 1,000 words: baseline, before and after flame graphs, each change with its measured effect, one dead end that did not help, and what you would monitor in production.
project.stretch: Rewrite the hottest loop in Rust or Go (as a CLI or a Python extension via PyO3) and measure whether the extra speed justifies the added build complexity.

exam.prompt: A test fails about 1 run in 20 on CI and never locally. Which first step best follows the scientific method?
options: Add `time.sleep(1)` to the test
Mark the test as flaky and skip it

Form a specific hypothesis (for example, the test depends on dict or test ordering, or on the current time), predict what would make it fail every time, and run that experiment, such as running the test in random order or with a frozen clock
Rewrite the test from scratch
exam.explain: A testable hypothesis with a prediction turns a rare failure into a reproducible one, which is the precondition for a real fix. Skipping hides the bug, a sleep is a guess that may mask a race, and rewriting the test throws away the evidence.

exam.prompt: In `git bisect run`, which exit codes mark a commit as **bad**?
options: Only 125
Any non-zero code including 255
Any code from 1 to 127 except 125
Only 1
exam.explain: 0 is good, 125 is skip, and 1 to 127 otherwise is bad. Codes above 127, such as 255, abort the bisect instead of marking the commit, so a script that can exit with them needs care.

exam.prompt: A flame graph of a slow endpoint shows `handle_request` spanning the full width. Above it, `render_template` is 15% wide, and `json.dumps` is 70% wide with no boxes above it. What should you investigate first?
options: `render_template`, because templates are usually slow
The `json.dumps` call: it accounts for about 70% of samples and is doing the work itself; check what is being serialized and whether it needs to be (huge payloads, repeated serialization)
Whatever function appears leftmost
`handle_request`, because it is the widest box
exam.explain: `handle_request` is wide only because everything runs inside it. A wide box with nothing above it is where CPU is actually being spent. Templates being "usually slow" is a guess the profile contradicts, and horizontal position is alphabetical, not meaningful.

exam.prompt: A bug report says every retry handler uses the last delay. Predict the output.
exam.code:
handlers = [lambda: i * 10 for i in range(3)]
print([h() for h in handlers])
exam.explain: Each lambda looks up `i` when it is called, not when it is created, and by then the comprehension has finished with `i` equal to 2. All three return 20. Binding the current value with a default argument, `lambda i=i: i * 10`, gives `[0, 10, 20]`. This late-binding behaviour is a classic reason to test the hypothesis instead of trusting the code's appearance.

exam.prompt: A user emails a screenshot of a 500 error page from yesterday. Which setup lets you find out exactly what went wrong for that request?
options: Printing stack traces to the terminal of whoever is running the server
An error page that shows a request ID, structured logs that include that ID on every line, and traces keyed by the same ID
Average latency metrics for the endpoint
Asking the user to reproduce it while you watch
exam.explain: The request ID links the user's report to the exact log lines and trace for that request, which is the core of observability. Averages describe all requests, not this one. Terminal output is lost and unsearchable, and many production failures cannot be reproduced on demand.

exam.prompt: Your team squash-merges every PR, and a recent PR was 3,000 lines touching 40 files. A regression appeared in that release. How does this affect finding it, and what does it suggest?
options: Squash merges prevent bisect from running at all
Bisect works better with large commits because there are fewer steps
It makes no difference to debugging

`git bisect` can only narrow it down to the whole 3,000-line commit, leaving a big manual search; smaller PRs, or keeping meaningful commits instead of squashing large ones, make bisect point to a small, readable change

exam.prompt: A colleague's benchmark shows a new JSON parser is 3x faster. It was timed once, on a 2 KB file, immediately after the module was imported. Production parses 40 MB files. What is the best response?
options: Merge it; 3x is a big win
Ask for repeated runs that exclude import and warm-up, on production-sized files, reported as a distribution, with a check that both parsers produce identical output
Reject it, because benchmarks are never reliable
Ask them to run it once more on the same 2 KB file to confirm
exam.explain: The benchmark has three pitfalls at once: a single run, warm-up included, and unrealistic data size, where a different complexity or memory profile may dominate at 40 MB. Fixing them is cheap and decides the question. Rejecting all benchmarks, or rerunning the same flawed one, does not.

exam.prompt: What is the key difference between deterministic and sampling profilers?
options: There is no difference; they are two names for the same thing
Sampling profilers only work in compiled languages
Deterministic profilers record every function call (exact counts, higher overhead); sampling profilers record the stack periodically (statistical, low overhead, can attach to running processes)
Deterministic profilers are always more accurate about where time goes
exam.explain: cProfile instruments every call, which gives exact counts but slows the program and can distort timings for small, frequently called functions. Sampling profilers like py-spy trade exact counts for low overhead and are available for Python, Go, Rust and more.
